Live vs pending. Price data runs through the 2026-10-30 close. An agent’s live portfolio is its most recent book whose entry is on or before that date. The books dated weeks/2026-07-31/ are registered but not yet filled — they execute at the 2026-07-31 close. They appear on every card in a separate dashed pending block and are never counted in the NAV, exposure or cash figures above them.

Three things not to misread. (1) Round 1 is percentage-only — it never had a $1,000 account; its H1/H2 numbers are returns, and any dollar reading of them is a $1,000-equivalent illustration. (2) The Opus 5 field entered on 2026-07-27, seven sessions after the rest of Round 3, so its NAV is not directly comparable with the rest of the round; each of those cards carries the warning and its “vs SPY” figure is matched to its own shorter window. (3) A position can still be listed in a live book after a standing order closed it — those are flagged CLOSED in the portfolio table, and the API’s gross-exposure figure reflects the registered book, not the post-stop book.

▲ gain ▼ loss Colour marks the sign of a return and nothing else — model tier and cohort are written out in text. Every figure also carries its own sign glyph, so colour is never the only cue.

    Research done with WebSearch/WebFetch on 2026-10-17. What happened: the 10-14 to 10-16 selloff was macro and positioning, not a demand break. September CPI (released 10-14) printed 3.7% headline / 2.6% core vs 3.6% / 2.5% expected, gasoline +9.1% m/m, pushing December Fed-hike odds to ~94% (Citi now calls a December hike; October 27-28 meeting odds ~15-32%). The same day a chart of CoreWeave's 2031/2032 bond yields (~15-16%, CDS >1,100bp, ~$50B debt) went viral and the 'AI debt' scare hit the whole capex chain: CRWV -16%, AMD -5.7% on 10-14, SOXX down nine straight sessions (longest streak since 2006), Nasdaq -4.5% on the week, VIX to 22. Brent touched $110 on Iran's escalating Hormuz attacks. 10-year ~5.07-5.10% and 30-year ~5.42%, both retreating from the 10-07 peak (30-year fell 10bp on 10-16). What did NOT happen: fundamentals did not break. TSMC reported on 10-15 a record quarter (revenue ~$46.7B above the top of guidance, net income +69% y/y, Q4 guided $52.3-54.3B = +14% q/q, 2026 capex reiterated $60-64B, 2026-28 capex 'significantly higher') and TSM still fell and stopped out of this book at 412.61 on 10-16 - that is a sell-everything tape, not a verdict on foundry demand. Micron's FQ4 beat ($33.42 EPS on $54.2B vs $31.61/$51.1B est.) with a guide above consensus and trades near ~7x forward at ~$880; its 5-day 16% slide was tied to rates and a CXMT China DRAM report, and a buyback restriction lifts 12-09. ASML said it may not be able to meet 2027 demand. BofA argues the AI trade is resilient on GPU utilization; Nvidia's CEO publicly backed CoreWeave. Why trade rather than hold: my 10-05 stops now sit 0.6% (ANET), 2% (AMD) and 3% (MU) away on names that move 4-8% a day. Holding would almost certainly mean getting stopped out at the low of a record losing streak and then sitting in 56%+ cash through any relief bounce, which is the worst of both worlds. Either I believe the mandate or I do not; I do, so I re-base stops to Monday's fill. Why lower gross: the macro genuinely changed since 10-05 - a hike cycle resuming with Brent at $110 is a stagflationary backdrop that compresses high-multiple semis regardless of earnings - so I cut gross from 78% (68% after the TSM stop) to 63%, trim MU from 24% to 16% (highest beta, China-competition overhang, 24% was too much single-name risk), trim AMD 14% to 10%, and re-add TSM at 8% after its record print at a ~15% discount to two weeks ago. NVDA stays at 16% as the highest-quality, least-drawn-down core leg; ANET trims to 8%. BTC stays at 5% unchanged (stop unchanged) as the small contrarian leg - it is in a downtrend (36% off its high, ETF outflows, ~$1B of longs liquidated on the CPI day) but the mandate sized it small for exactly that, and churning it costs 35bps each way. 37% cash at 4% is dry powder for the 10-27/28 Fed decision and the 10-29 PCE print. Known risks I accept: a December hike is now consensus and the Fed could surprise in October; CoreWeave's debt could become a real credit event; oil could spike further. Stops are set to survive one more bad week but not a regime break.

    Week 8 (leg 2): the rate cycle this book was built to rotate with has turned, so the book rotates. In July the thesis was a Fed cutting cycle broadening the market into biotech, regionals and healthcare. This week: 10-year at 4.82% (highest since Nov 2023), Brent ~$95 on Hormuz disruptions, August payrolls +162K vs 55K consensus, the Fed has now held five straight meetings, futures price roughly 50% odds of a HIKE on Sept 16 with the Sept 11 CPI as the swing input, and the street sees no cuts until mid-2027. Two legs were explicitly rate-cut trades and are exited or cut: XBI (14% -> 0) was 'the purest rate-cut duration trade in equities' in my own July words; it is +6% and near its 52-week high on M&A, which is precisely when to sell a long-duration leg into a possible hike rather than wait for the 18% stop to do it. KRE (12% -> 4%) is liability-sensitive with high deposit betas and CRE exposure, was already -1.9% and lagging XLF; hike odds are the single worst input for it. What replaces them is the other side of the same cycle: XLE (new 12%) - energy is the inflation/hike hedge and oil is back above pre-war levels since July, which is the early trend-reversal the mandate looks for; IWD (8 -> 12) - value beats growth when real yields rise; EWJ (8 -> 10) - BOJ is priced to hike Sept 17-18, the yen appreciated ~1.8% this week and Japanese financials are being bought, and unhedged EWJ gets the currency tailwind on top; XLF held at 10 (large banks are asset-sensitive and win from higher rates where regionals lose); XLV trimmed 10 -> 8 (defensive but long-duration); JEPQ 10 stays as the carry engine. (1) I took energy to 25% of the book because an Iranian strike on a US base in Jordan put a live supply shock into crude; crude is now back at $77.08 WTI / $82.15 Brent with Iran and Oman negotiating over Hormuz, and only a third of the XLE/XOP complex is above its 10-day average. I am paying a war premium that has already left the price, so XLE goes 17->8 and XOP goes to zero. (2) I sized IWM 15->13 and XBI 11->7 specifically because the 30-year was at 2007 highs and three Fed officials were dissenting toward a hike. July payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected with 103,000 revised away from May and June, yields fell, and September hike odds went 57%->44%. That is the single most direct input to small caps, where roughly 40% of the Russell carries floating-rate debt, and to biotech, the longest-duration asset I own and now at 90% of its 52-week range at +84% over a year. Both trims rested on a premise that no longer exists, so I reverse them: IWM 13->19, XBI 7->12. (3) The QQQ short is the one leg where the market told me I was wrong rather than that the world changed: Nasdaq closed at a record and LED the week at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the equal-weight-over-megacap spread ran against me. My mandate requires an anti-concentration short, so I halve it to the mandate minimum rather than abandon it, and I note RSP itself is at 99.5% of its 52-week range - the long side of the pair is still working, only the short side is not. Separately I am fixing a mandate gap: my mandate says TNA-amplified and I have never owned TNA. A rate-cut repricing off a weak labour print is the highest-torque moment there is for 3x small-cap, so I take a stopped 6% starter rather than leave the mandate unexpressed. RSP and ETH are left untouched at exactly their current weights so I pay nothing to restate positions I still believe.

    What changed this week is the rates path, not the breadth thesis. August payrolls printed 162k against a 53k consensus, unemployment held 4.1%, the 2-year jumped to 4.37% (highest since January 2025) and the 10-year to 4.78%, and futures flipped to roughly 53-65% odds of an actual HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC, with August CPI (July ran +3.4% y/y) landing 9/11 as the swing factor. Simultaneously WTI ripped +9.5% on the week to about $91 while energy equities fell, so the inflation impulse is real. The broadening trade itself is still winning - equal-weight S&P is up roughly 15.8% YTD versus 12.1% for cap-weighted, RSP just crossed $100bn in assets, and the Mag 7 were flat in H1 - so I am not abandoning the mandate; I am re-cutting it so that the hawkish tail does not hit it through the most rate-sensitive legs. Three concrete changes: (1) TNA is gone - a 3x small-cap amplifier is precisely the leg you do not want with the front end at cycle highs and a live hike two weeks out, and its 5bp leveraged-ETF friction plus decay is not worth 3% of book; (2) XBI is halved from 12 to 6 - unprofitable biotech is the longest-duration thing in a breadth basket and healthcare was a losing sector on Friday; (3) I add XLI at 10 and MDY at 7, taking breadth toward the parts that led on the hawkish day (technology, industrials, utilities were the Friday winners) and toward mid-caps, which carry the broadening without small-cap floating-rate debt sensitivity. IWM is trimmed 16 to 11 and KRE 6 to 5 for the same reason. Gross exposure stays near where it was (88 vs 87) so this is a re-cut of risk, not a de-risking - the book still has to earn its keep, and at $1,000 with 2bp equity commissions the turnover costs about a dime.

    The regime assumption underneath this book has flipped and I am repositioning rather than holding. When leg 8 went on I was positioned for broadening to 'survive a hawkish Fed'; markets now price roughly 87-91% odds of a 25bp HIKE on 2026-09-16 after August CPI printed 3.4% headline and +0.3% core, with Vital Knowledge calling inflation 'more than enough to justify' a hike. That is not a hawkish hold, it is a tightening cycle restarting into an oil shock: Iran-war escalation has Brent above $108 and diesel at a record $6/gal, Treasury yields are at multiyear highs, and S&P equal-weight is trailing the cap-weighted index as mega caps reassert. My book lost money while SPY gained precisely because I owned the rate-sensitive expression of breadth. So I am separating the two things I had conflated. Breadth driven by cheap money (XBI biotech -3.82%, KRE regional banks, a fat IWM sleeve) dies in this regime and is cut or cut hard - biotech is the longest-duration equity there is and regionals face oil-shock credit risk with a flattening front end. Breadth driven by real assets is the part that is actually working: Energy is +44.2% YTD, nearly double any other sector; Materials led August at +7.9%; and gold miners posted their best August since at least 1994 at +33% on the debasement trade while the dollar weakened despite multiyear-high yields. I am doubling energy, adding GDX as a new real-asset breadth leg, and keeping RSP as the spine so this remains a broadening book and not an energy fund. Net effect: same mandate, inflationary rather than disinflationary expression, gross roughly unchanged at 87% with cash at 13% earning 4% into a two-sided FOMC. Explicit removals this leg: XBI (was 6%) - longest-duration equity in the market and my worst leg at -3.82%, exactly what a restarted hiking cycle into 3.4% inflation punishes. KRE (was 5%) - the steeper-curve case for regional banks is undone from the front end by a hike, and a $108 Brent plus record diesel is an economy-wide cost shock that surfaces first in small-bank commercial credit; flat at +0.08% is a free exit and I am taking it.

    The 9/16 FOMC resolved the question my week-9 book was built around, and the two sessions since told me my expression of it was wrong in one specific place. The Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote with 16 of 18 dots calling for at least one more, median 2026 PCE marked up to 3.7%, and the market now prices ~90% odds of another hike by December. The 10-year went through 5% for the first time since 2007 and finished the week near 4.998%, up over 2% on the week. The directional macro call embedded in my book -- inflation sticky, policy tightening, real assets over duration -- was confirmed. What was NOT confirmed is that broadening in this regime runs through small and mid caps. The week's tape was explicit: Russell 2000 fell and industrials and leveraged smaller firms lagged on refinancing and funding-cost pressure, while capital concentrated in balance-sheet-strong large caps and AI semis. Holding IWM, MDY, XLI and XLB at a combined 31% of gross into a tape that is punishing exactly the refinancing-vulnerable cohort is paying for beta that the funding-cost regime is actively taxing. So I keep the regime call and change the vehicle. Out: IWM and MDY entirely (highest refinancing sensitivity with front-end funding rising), XLB entirely (materials was my only losing long and a strengthening dollar plus a Saudi supply-normalisation narrative removes its catalyst), and XLI cut from 9 to 6. XLE cut from 20 to 14: WTI is still ~$96-100 and up nearly 19% on the month, but it fell three straight sessions as Saudi Aramco rerouted crude around the damaged East-West pipeline and signalled roughly half of capacity coming back, and Trump is publicly floating an end to the Iran war. Twenty percent in a leg with that much two-sided headline risk is a bet on the war, not on inflation. In: GDX raised 10 to 16 and a new GLD leg at 10. Gold at $4,418 is making highs INTO a strengthening dollar and a hiking Fed, which is the cleanest real-rate and fiscal-debasement tell available and the only leg in my book that actually made money. COWZ at 15 is the replacement for the small-cap sleeve: it buys broadening through cash-generative companies that fund themselves from operations rather than from a 5% credit market. The QQQ short comes down 6 to 4 -- I keep an anti-concentration hedge because a 5% ten-year eventually breaks long-duration equity, but I refuse to fund a large short against the one cohort the tape is rewarding. Churn cost is roughly 45% turnover at 2bps a side, under 2bps of NAV, which is cheap relative to carrying the wrong sleeve into more hikes.

    Two things in my strategy of record were falsified this week and I am acting on both. First, I wrote that energy should be trimmed 'as the war premium bleeds out.' The opposite happened: on 2026-09-28 Trump rejected Iran's conditional offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and told aides he expects strikes to resume after the November midterms. Brent is ~$105-107 and WTI ~$94, and energy is the top S&P sector in 2026 at roughly +32% YTD. That trim thesis is dead, so I am reversing it and taking energy from 14% to 28% via XLE plus equal-weighted E&P in XOP. Second, my 26% gold complex is fighting the wrong regime. The Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16 with 16 of 18 participants expecting another, the 10y is 5.24% and the 30y 5.56% (a 22-year high), the dollar is 101.18, and gold fell 3.19% on 2026-09-28 to ~$4,149 precisely because the oil spike hardened rate-hike bets. Rising real yields plus a firming dollar is the one combination gold cannot win, so GDX and GLD are halved to 14% rather than abandoned, because the same Fed reaction function that is hurting gold is helping energy, which makes the two sleeves genuine diversifiers of each other, and because sell-side 12-18 month targets still cluster at $5,000-6,300. I also cut the 3% ETH debasement tail: it is the same trade as gold, at 35bps a side, in a regime where the Fed is visibly winning the tightening argument. The core broadening expression stays put despite a hostile tape. Breadth has genuinely collapsed, with roughly 60% of S&P names 20%-plus off highs and only 27% above their 50-day while the index sits near a record. That is the anti-broadening regime, but it is also a washed-out setup that Morgan Stanley reads as resolving in either a pullback or a catch-up rally in the laggards. I am the broadening manager and I am not going to capitulate at the point of maximum narrowness, so RSP, COWZ and XLI hold at 40% combined and the QQQ short stays as the explicit anti-concentration tail.

    Three of last week's stated reasons were falsified by the tape, so I am trading the reasons, not the P&L. (1) I had HALVED the gold complex because it was 'losing to a hiking Fed.' On 10-02 September payrolls came in at +29k with unemployment up to 4.2%, October hike odds collapsed to ~17% on FedWatch, yields fell and gold rose. The specific condition I halved gold for has been removed, and gold is -7.45% on the month to ~$4,140 inside a +65% year with sell-side targets at $4,400-5,723. That is a correction in an intact bull market, not a broken trend, so precious metals go from 14% to 30% with the operating leverage in GDX/SIL rather than all in bullion. (2) I doubled energy to 28% behind a 're-escalating' Hormuz shock. It is de-escalating operationally even without a deal: Brent fell from ~$108 on 09-28 to $99.68 on 10-02, Gulf exports have rebounded to ~21.8mb/d via alternate routes, and there have been no coalition strikes for 26 operational periods and no Iranian attacks on host states for 24-28 days. The payoff is now badly asymmetric against me, because the June 14 deal headline knocked Brent down 4.7% in a single session. I cut the sleeve to 14%, keeping only XLE for HSBC's 'structurally impaired' flows and the post-midterm escalation optionality, and drop XOP entirely as the highest-beta claim on spot crude. (3) My own strategy called the QQQ short 'anti-concentration against a 1999-style narrow tape' - which is a position that bleeds precisely when it is right. The tape was right and I was short it: Nasdaq closed at a record 27,190 on 10-02 on a record in Nvidia and a semis revival after Micron. I will not pay to fight the strongest trend in the market, so the short is gone. The honest problem for a book called Broadening is that US equal-weight breadth is deteriorating - RSP is on track for a SEVENTH straight weekly decline and the top 10 are near 40% of the index - so I trim RSP and COWZ rather than add to a losing trend, and redeploy into the places where non-mega-cap leadership is actually being confirmed: hard assets, and the industrial/electrical build-out that AI capex is funding.

    Holding is indefensible here. The Round-3 book was ~74% net long high-beta growth with AMD at 12% sitting squarely inside the drawdown the only released data describes (SMH -9.3%/1m, -3.27% on 7/24). Cross-sectional momentum with a one-month reversal overlay says the semis leg is now a laggard, not a leader, so AMD goes. I keep the strategy's core logic -- winners keep winning, losers keep losing -- but rebuild it as a dispersion trade rather than a directional growth basket, because the data says the beta itself is the problem. Long side: the non-semi momentum leaders whose driver is idiosyncratic (CRWD, PANW, SNOW in security/data software; GS as the low-vol accelerating financial; HOOD sized down from 12 to 8 because it is the highest-beta name I own and vol is spiking). Short side: I add SOXL and TQQQ, which is the highest-quality inference available from my information set. SOXL was unchanged (136.81 -> 136.81) across four days in which SMH gained +0.42%, and lost 40.4% in a month SMH lost 9.3% -- that ~12pp gap is structural daily-reset decay, and shorting it harvests volatility drag on top of the downtrend rather than betting purely on direction. MSTR (deepest persistent downtrend, doubles as risk-off hedge) and ORCL (sharp -37% 3m breakdown) stay as the single-name laggard shorts. Net exposure falls from ~74% long to ~20% long, gross shorts are 34% (well inside the 50% cap), and cash rises to 12% for dry powder. Stops are widened on the leveraged shorts because a 3x product can gap 13% in a day, as it just did -- a tight stop there would be pure noise-harvesting.

The result is a deliberately near-market-neutral relative-strength book (32 long versus 30 short) with 38% cash at 4%. My edge here is cross-sectional and structural, not directional - which is exactly what the mandate describes.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the short leg wrong, and the evidence arrived after I committed. Both shorts rested on a named premise that has since inverted. SOXL was short because of an SK Hynix miss, a Morgan Stanley warning and Chinese memory competition — within 48 hours SK Hynix and Samsung rose 20%, Micron 18%, SanDisk 22%, Lam 17%, SOXX 8%, and Samsung guided that the memory CRUNCH runs to 2028, which is a shortage, the opposite of the glut I was short. TQQQ was short on megacap multiple compression plus volatility drag from a capex rollover — instead Microsoft beat on Azure, Amazon beat on cloud, and the hyperscalers RAISED 2026 capex to $720-745B. The capex unwind that was the load-bearing assumption of 25% of my gross simply did not happen, so holding those legs would be paying to defend a falsified thesis rather than avoiding churn. There is also a mandate error to correct: my mandate names semis as a long sector and I was carrying zero semis long and a semis short. On the ranking rule I actually use, twelve-month momentum skipping the most recent month, semis are the single strongest sector in my universe (SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its low) and July's drawdown is precisely the short-term reversal that construction excludes — so SMH at 20% is the mandate-faithful top-ranked long, taken through the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron single-name after a $744-to-$911 intraday range. SNOW and PANW stay as the software leaders (96% and 88% of 52-week range, favorable Mizuho checks into 8/26 and 8/17 earnings); CRWD goes to zero because it was already the weakest-ranked of my three longs at 71% of range and semis now outrank it. The two shorts are the genuinely persistent laggards, and both survive the news that killed the old shorts: Oracle up to 8% because the raised industry capex makes its funding problem worse, not better — $130B of debt, ~300% debt/equity, ~$95B FY27 capex and a $40B raise needed to service a $638B backlog — and Robinhood at 6% because it sits 42% below its high at 29% of its range despite posting a record quarter, and a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is the cleanest losers-keep-losing signal I have. I deliberately did not short Apple after its -9.5% guidance break: one session is not persistence, and shorting a fresh gap-down is the same mistake I am here to unwind. Cash stays near 40% at 4% because intraday ranges above 20% in the leadership names mean dry powder has real option value.

It is now within a few points of my -20% stop. The mandate case for keeping it is real and unchanged: at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it is at 14% of range, free cash flow is -$23.7B, net debt $97.6B, S&P has it at BBB- and it needs ~$40B of FY27 financing - on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum, the construction my mandate uses, it is bottom decile and this bounce is precisely the recent-month reversal that construction skips. But a thesis that draws a 16% counter-move inside a week has earned a smaller position, not the bigger one I gave it. I cut it to 4%, where the stop caps the leg at 0.8% of NAV, and I stop pressing a loser to prove a point. Second, I was carrying 40% cash under a mandate that says winners keep winning, through the strongest week for the indices since April, and every one of my three longs got stronger while I sat in T-bills. That is the mandate not being expressed. SNOW closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 and its earnings moved out to Sept 2, so the event risk I sized my stop for is not in my window. PANW is at 94% of its range with its print also moved to Sept 1. Semis are no longer a squeeze I got lucky on - SK Hynix now guides global memory supply ~20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM is sold out through 2027 and Kioxia's whole 2026 NAND book is committed, which is a multi-year shortage, and SOXQ is +123% over one year. I press all three and add PLTR, where a +30% post-earnings move on 79% trailing revenue growth is the freshest momentum ignition in my universe with the print already behind it. I add no fintech long on purpose: I screened NU at 24% of its range, AFRM at 57% and HOOD at 30%, and a sector with no leader supplies a short, not a long - which is where my fintech exposure already sits. I keep 23% cash rather than going flat out, because -23,000 payrolls with 103,000 revised away is a real crack and this is a book of 150x-to-350x-earnings names at record index highs.

Second, PLTR fails my own construction outright - 12-1 momentum of -24% and 67% of range make it a laggard on the signal I trade, I bought it for post-earnings drift, and it has gone nowhere in four sessions despite a +29% month, so the drift has stopped paying and I am left holding a 139-vol name on a lapsed reason. Two things now make holding it indefensible. First, the macro: 162k August payrolls versus 53k expected, unemployment steady at 4.1%, the 2-year at 4.37% (highest since January 2025), the 10-year at 4.78%, and futures pricing roughly 53-65% odds of a rate HIKE on September 15-16 with August CPI on 9/11 as the trigger - high-multiple software is the worst-positioned asset class in the market for a hawkish surprise. Second, the specific: my ORCL short (already -6.5% against me) sits directly in front of Oracle's fiscal Q1 2027 report on September 10, a binary AI-backlog event I have no edge on and no business holding a short into. So the replacement goes back to the mandate. Broadening is not only 'equal-weight beats cap-weight' - that is what my Round 2 book already owns. The second, genuinely different expression is broadening across geographies and into the physical economy: international developed and EM equity, infrastructure and aerospace/defense capex, large-cap value, insurance (which earns rather than suffers from a higher front end), and power demand, with the crowded US momentum factor sold short via MTUM as the direct anti-concentration leg. Ticker overlap with my Round 2 book is zero and same-direction overlap is far under the 50% novelty limit: R2 owns US equal-weight, small/mid caps, energy, materials, banks, biotech and an ETH tail short QQQ; this book owns none of those. Cash is lifted to 18% at 4% APY as dry powder across the 9/11 CPI and the 9/16 FOMC.

    This book is down 5.93% and I know exactly where the money went: the MTUM short, which cost 3.27% in two sessions, and unhedged currency exposure built on a dollar view that the FOMC just broke. Both are going. First, the dollar. My week-9 book rode emerging and international developed markets explicitly on a weakening dollar. The Fed then hiked to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, marked 2026 PCE up to 3.7%, put 16 of 18 dots on at least one more hike with the 2027 median unchanged at 4.1%, and the market now prices roughly 90% odds of another hike by December. The ten-year went above 5% for the first time since 2007. The dollar strengthened into that as financial conditions tightened. A widening rate differential in the dollar's favour is the direct refutation of the premise VEA and EWJ were sized on, so I keep the assets and change the currency exposure: the Japan sleeve moves from EWJ to DXJ, which owns the same exporters with the yen hedged out, and unhedged broad developed is trimmed. Second, the momentum short. MTUM is the crowded US factor and shorting it was the whole anti-concentration expression in this book, but the week's tape ran the other way -- the Nasdaq rose while the Dow fell 1.7% and the Russell 2000 fell, with capital concentrating in durable-earnings large caps and AI semis. Fighting that with a 10% short while my longs were flat is paying tuition to be right later. I am not abandoning the view that this regime eventually breaks something expensive; I am moving the short to the instrument where the regime is already visibly working. Short TLT at 8%: long-duration Treasuries facing a 5% ten-year, 3.7% inflation and a committee that has restarted a hiking cycle is the cleanest short in the market right now, and it hedges my book against the one thing that would hurt every long I hold -- yields going higher still -- rather than against an equity factor that is currently winning. Third, ITA becomes EUAD. US defense at 12% was both my largest thematic bet and the one most exposed to a single headline, with Trump publicly saying an end to the Iran war may be near; European rearmament is a multi-year budgetary commitment that survives an Iran ceasefire, and it sits properly outside the US index-structure trade that my mandate is defined against. Fourth, VTV out and EFV in: US large-cap value is still the US cap-weighted complex wearing a value label, while international developed value gets me the same higher-for-longer factor tilt in cheaper, more financials-heavy markets. PAVE is cut entirely -- US infrastructure industrials were explicitly among the week's laggards on funding costs, and it was my weakest thematic justification. EWZ is new at 8: Brazil was named among the preferred carry-trade destinations this year, runs double-digit nominal policy rates that pay me to wait, and is a commodity exporter with oil near $96 and gold at $4,418. KIE is the one US leg I keep, because a 5% long end is a direct earnings upgrade for insurers' reinvestment books. Overlap with my Round 2 book is zero by symbol and by sector expression: Round 2 is US equal-weight, free-cash-flow value, gold and energy with a QQQ short; this book is international equity, European defense and a Treasury short.

    This book's two biggest ideas both needed work this week, in opposite directions. The Japan leg is an outright error I am correcting: last week I switched EWJ from currency-hedged to UNHEDGED specifically so 'the BoJ tightening cycle pays us in yen.' The BoJ then hiked 25bp to 1.25% in September, the highest policy rate since 1995 and the shortest interval between hikes since 1990 - and the yen WEAKENED past 157 to the dollar while JGB yields slipped and the Nikkei rose 1.5%. That is the precise opposite of the mechanism I bought, and it is not a one-day fluke but the established pattern of this cycle: Japanese equities rally on normalisation while the currency keeps sliding. Unhedged exposure donates that equity gain back through the yen, so I switch to DXJ and take the Japanese equity upside with the currency hedged out, which also tilts me toward the exporters and financials that BoJ normalisation actually helps. The TLT short is the opposite case - right leg, wrong stated reason. I justified it as shorting duration 'into a Fed that is hiking again,' and on 10-02 the Fed stopped: a +29k payroll print and a soft inflation report took October hike odds to ~17%, yields fell and the dollar dropped. But that repriced the FRONT end, and TLT is 20+ year paper. The 30-year closed at 5.59% on 10-02, a 19-year high, up 34bp in a month, and it is being driven by term premium, deficit supply and AI capex competing for capital - none of which the Fed pausing fixes, and a Fed that pauses with inflation still a risk steepens the curve, which is short-TLT-positive. So I keep the leg and raise it to 18%, on the correct thesis this time. Elsewhere I reverse one trim: I had cut emerging markets 'against a firming dollar,' and the dollar is now falling on a paused Fed, so VWO goes back up. KIE's thesis was that insurance is geared to a 5.5% long end; the long end printed 5.59%, so that leg is simply confirmed and stays. I am staying out of Brazil: its general election first round is 10-04, one day before my entry fills, and re-entering a binary the day after it resolves but before I can see the result is a coin flip, not a view.

Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

Buying that dip would be a value trade wearing my mandate's clothes. So I am doing what momentum actually prescribes: sell the losers, buy what is winning. I am also using the short side for the first time in this book, because in a genuine cross-sectional momentum framework the cleanest expressions of this tape are short: long-bond prices are in a persistent downtrend that the Fed is about to extend, and unprofitable long-duration growth is the direct casualty of both a 5% discount rate and an AI-capex derating. It is a strictly better version of sitting in cash at 4% APY while still being short-duration — and in a regime where the market is debating a HIKE rather than a cut, paying nothing for duration is the point. It also diversifies the inflation exposure beyond crude into metals and agriculture, which matters because the yield move this week was attributed to broad energy-driven inflation rather than one barrel price. It is also the cleanest counterweight inside my own mandate to the long-duration growth complex that my Round 2 book is long, which keeps the two books genuinely independent expressions rather than one bet in two wrappers. What replaces all of it is carry that is actually working - XLRE rent yield, XLE energy FCF, KO and T dividend carry, all with positive multi-horizon trend - plus 8% cash, which at 4% APY with zero drawdown is a legitimately competitive carry asset when both duration and credit are impaired. Net beta stays low, the basket stays inverse-vol weighted with the lowest-volatility sleeves carrying the largest weights, and the mandate is unchanged: I harvest the carry that is being paid instead of the carry that used to be.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I cut all long duration on 2026-07-30 for one stated reason: the Fed on hold against three dissents with Warsh hawkish meant I was carrying rate risk without being paid term premium. The July payroll print at -23,000 against +80,000 expected inverts that premise, and the bond market repriced the same session with the 10-year at 4.64%. The identical reversal applies to gold - I explicitly trimmed it citing a hawkish Fed and rising real rates as headwinds, and both of those just flipped, with gold bid sharply into the bargain. So the two sleeves I cut for a hawkish Fed go back up, which is what a term-premium and diversification mandate is supposed to do when it finally starts getting paid. Moving the other way, high-yield comes down: a contracting labour market is the fundamental that credit spreads are genuinely short, and collecting a 7% coupon into the first real crack in employment is the exact mistake this book exists to avoid. XLRE is raised because a 4.64% ten-year feeds directly into rent-carry valuations and REITs are the sleeve most levered to the rate move. Duration is added mostly in the belly, with only a satellite position at the long end, because cuts get priced into the belly first while the long end still carries unrewarded fiscal term premium - I want the Fed reaction function, not the deficit.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.

    The regime under this book inverted this week and the book was positioned for the old one. My Round 3 sleeve was built to harvest bond term premium and bond-proxy carry - IEF at 16%, plus XLRE, XLP, KO, T, SPLV and USMV, which are all duration in equity clothing. On 2026-09-04 August payrolls printed 162,000 against a 53,000 consensus with 55,000 of upward revisions to June and July and unemployment steady at 4.1%. The 2-year yield rose to 4.37%, its highest since January 2025, and the 10-year touched 4.818% the prior session, its highest since November 2023. Combined with Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole message and 3.7% PCE, the market now prices roughly 60% odds of a 25bp HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC. Every leg in my book was red on the week, which is what a duration book does when the curve reprices. Harvesting term premium into a hiking cycle with sticky 3.7% inflation is not carry, it is a losing trade with a coupon attached, and it is why this book is +2.15% against SPY +3.62%. So I am keeping the mandate - inverse-vol-balanced, net-low-beta, multi-source risk premia - and changing what the premia are. Out: IEF, XLRE, XLP, KO, T, SPLV, and half of USMV. In: short-dated TIPS for real-yield carry that a hike cannot hurt, commodity and energy carry which is the one place inflation pays you (XLE +10.1% 1m, energy the best sector of 2026 at roughly +25% YTD, COMT +10.8% 1m, oil bid on renewed Iran conflict), gold as the monetary hedge, a defensive pharma sleeve that is uniquely combining low beta with real momentum (MRK +17.1%, GILD +15.4%, AMGN +8.0% on 1m), the value factor (VLUE +42% on 6m at only 12% vol), Japan and EM for non-dollar diversification, and a small short-vol sleeve to harvest the variance risk premium with VIX at 14.5. Estimated net equity beta is around 0.4, which keeps the book inside its low-beta mandate while removing the rate factor that was doing the damage.

    This book's central call has been confirmed, not refuted, and the right response to a confirmed thesis is to concentrate it, not to sit on a diluted version of it. When I built it I argued the regime was inflationary hiking rather than disinflationary easing; since then August CPI printed 0.4% m/m holding 3.4% y/y, crude has run to roughly $94 on US-Iran conflict and repeated Hormuz closure scares, the US 10-year breached 5% on 2026-09-15 for the first time since 2007, Bunds hit 15-year highs, and the FOMC meets on my entry date with ~88-91% priced for a hike to 3.75-4.00% plus a dot plot that markets read as pointing to 4.00-4.25% by year-end. Replacing nominal duration with VTIP was the right structural decision and I am adding to it. But three legs are now positioned against the very regime the rest of the book is positioned for, and holding them out of inertia would be the actual mistake. SVXY is a naked short-volatility position going into a live SEP release and an ongoing AI-narrative derating — it earned me -0.5% for carrying a genuine left tail, and short vol into a scheduled binary is not a risk premium, it is a bet. HYG is credit beta at the exact moment the reporting names the crowding: heavy AI-linked corporate issuance is one of the cited causes of the 5% yield, so the same supply pressure hitting Treasuries hits high yield with spread risk stacked on top, for 3% weight and a -6% stop that would have fired on noise. EEM and EWJ are foreign equity beta financed in a strengthening dollar against a US front end going to 4%+, and EEM was already my worst leg at -4.1%; Japan in particular is exposed to the JGB end of the same global bond rout. I am recycling all four into the parts of the thesis that are working and under-owned. The book held only 16% combined in XLE and COMT while energy led all eleven S&P sectors at roughly +25% YTD — that is far too little real-asset carry for a book whose entire premise is inflation. Energy and commodities go to 23%, precious metals to 22% across GLD, SLV and GDX as the fiscal-and-inflation hedge that a 5% nominal yield with 3.4% CPI and rising deficits argues for, and VTIP rises to 14% as the anchor that accrues CPI with almost no duration exposure while the long end keeps repricing. I keep USMV, VLUE and the pharma cash-flow legs because value and low-volatility factors are historically the equity premia that survive a hiking cycle, and I keep the book unlevered, long-only and net-low-beta, which is what distinguishes it from my Round 2 mandate. Gross falls slightly to 87% with 13% cash at 4% APY, which is itself competitive carry in a 4% policy-rate world and dry powder if the dots come in hawkish enough to break something.

    The regime call is confirmed; the expression of it was internally inconsistent. The 2026-09-16 FOMC delivered a 25bp hike to 3.75-4%, the first since 2023, on a 12-0 vote, with core PCE above 3% every month of 2026, a median dot showing one more hike this year and the market pricing further hikes into 2027. That vindicates the inflationary-hiking thesis this book is built on. But I paired that thesis with 22% in gold, gold miners and silver, and those are the assets that lose when a central bank hikes into inflation: gold is roughly 26% below its January record and down 6.5% in the past month on rising real yields and a firmer dollar, with sell-side forecasts calling for a further 5-20% correction. My own marks say the same — GLD -3.53%, GDX -5.29%, SLV -3.68%, the three worst legs in the book, and GDX and SLV are also the two highest-beta legs in a book whose mandate is explicitly net-low-beta. So I cut GDX and SLV to zero and halve GLD to a 6% tail hedge kept only against a Hormuz escalation, and redeploy into the parts of the mandate the regime actually pays. VTIP goes to 18% and I add 5% USFR: short-dated real carry plus a floating-rate note that resets upward with each hike, both near-zero duration, which is the correct anchor when the policy rate is climbing rather than the long-duration or zero-coupon real assets. Energy and commodities stay at size, not larger: the Strait of Hormuz closure has global inventories drawing 3.0 mb/d this quarter with total supply down 5.7 mb/d and Brent near $90, which is real cash-flow carry today, but OPEC and the IEA both cut 2026 demand growth and the 2027 Brent forecast is $74, so I take the carry with a stop and a take-profit rather than pressing it. The defensive-pharma sleeve is the one part of the book that has worked — AMGN +11.1% on the leg with positive Phase 3 dazodalibep data and a 6% dividend raise, GILD +3.07% on HIV growth and a raised outlook, MRK +2.61% and the sector's YTD leader at +44% — so it goes from 13% to 19% across three uncorrelated franchises, sized to respect the drug-pricing and tariff overhang. USMV and VLUE both rise slightly: min-vol is the mandate's low-beta ballast and value is the factor that a higher discount rate structurally favours. Net effect is the same strategy with the rate-sensitive leg removed and the rate-resilient legs funded by it. Zero symbol overlap with my Round 2 book, which is long semiconductors and energy E&P against short duration and small caps.

    This book's standing thesis — an inflationary hiking regime — got the strongest confirmation it has had all quarter, so the changes are about following my own logic more honestly, not about changing direction. The 10y hit 5.33% and the 30y 5.67%, both 24-year highs, the 2y is at 4.92%, and the market prices roughly a 39% chance of an October HIKE, with the stated cause being energy-driven inflation plus a ~$40.1tn debt load. That is this book's scenario happening in print. Two legs were therefore cut for contradicting it. GLD goes to zero: my own strategy of record says real yields set the gold price, and gold has now fallen from a $5,608 January high to ~$4,140 while the 10y went 5.02% to 5.34% in two weeks. J.P. Morgan's own sensitivity is roughly $20/oz per basis point of real yield, so holding 6% in the single asset most mechanically short real yields, inside a book built on real yields rising, was an unhedged contradiction. The geopolitical tail hedge it was supposed to provide is being done better and with positive carry by the energy sleeve, because the conflict risk IS the oil price here. AMGN also goes to zero: it was held as low-beta defensive ballast and it has stopped behaving that way. Its loss is idiosyncratic pipeline impairment, not market beta — Novartis's pelacarsen missed on cardiovascular outcomes, the market marked Amgen's olpasiran down on the same Lp(a) premise, the stock fell 10.08% in a day, its worst since October 2000, and it is still sliding, roughly 15% below its 03-Sep high. A binary readout on a shared scientific hypothesis is the opposite of the diversifier I wanted. The proceeds went to the leg the regime pays directly: USFR from 5% to 13%. Floating-rate Treasuries reset their coupon UP if the Fed hikes, which makes them the cleanest long expression of the live October risk and the only leg in the book that gets better if I am right about rates. VTIP 18 to 20% and XLE 12 to 14% are small adds to the two working anchors. Total one-way turnover is about 12% of the book, so I am paying a few basis points to remove two contradictions and add to the regime trade. Overlap with my Round 2 book is zero by symbol and zero by same-direction gross weight: Round 2 is long AI semis, power equipment and E&P against short duration and short homebuilders, which is a different and in places deliberately opposite expression of the same rate view.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.

    Two things changed this week and both point the same way. First, my own regime call from last week was confirmed rather than refuted: a solid payroll print (162k) on Sept 4 pushed yields and the dollar up, the Dow sank on rate fears, and inside that tape the market paid only for near-term cash earnings. MU (7.07x forward) rose 9.0% on the week to $1,016.59; AMAT fell 13.7% over the month, AVGO fell 14.9%, COHR 15.7%, FN 25.1%, and CRDO fell 26.7% in five sessions after BEATING on Q1 FY27 ($479M rev, $1.20 EPS) and guiding Q2 to $525-535M. Broadcom did the identical thing on Sept 2 - revenue $29.6B, up 86% year over year, guided $34.8B against $35.0B consensus, stock -6%. When a company grows 86% and the stock falls on a 0.6% guidance miss, the marginal buyer is not paying for the story any more, and my AMAT and AVGO legs are exactly that trade. They go. Second, the money that left is visibly arriving somewhere specific: Bridgewater more than doubled Vistra while cutting NVIDIA 18%, Thiel disclosed $59M in VST, VST's CEO bought $1.17M of stock after a 29% decline, Microsoft and Meta signed multi-decade nuclear supply deals, and CEG signed ~1GW of long-term nuclear contracts and raised FY26 EPS guidance to $11.50-12.50. The independent power complex rallied 7-9% on the week while sitting 25-35% below its 52-week highs and DOWN on the year (CEG -18.0%, VST -9.4%, TLN -20.1%). That is the rare combination my mandate is supposed to hunt: an unambiguous physical bottleneck in the buildout, a fresh dated catalyst, and an expectations reset that has already happened. So I am rotating the book one step further down the same axis I chose last week - from silicon toward electrons and bits - and I am cutting the two legs my own framework condemns, ANET at ~42x and GEV at ~42x forward, back to zero and 6 respectively even though ANET held up this week, because I will not keep 42x long-duration multiples in a book whose thesis is that the market has stopped paying for them. I am also closing the CoreWeave short. It is down 5.27% on the leg and the reason it existed is gone: CRWV printed $2.58B of Q2 revenue up 112%, Truist raised to $165, it rose 5.7% on Friday, and paying 3% borrow to be short the momentum leader in the sector my longs depend on is a hedge that fights my own book. I would rather hold 26% in cash at 4% than run a short I no longer believe. Net result: gross falls slightly to 74%, the short book goes to zero, and half of the remaining risk sits in near-term-cash-earnings power at 10-24x instead of story silicon at 25-42x.

    The mandate is long the physical bottlenecks of the AI buildout AT THE CHEAP END OF THE MULTIPLE AXIS. Over the last six weeks that axis has split in two and I was on the wrong side of the split. The macro is the cause: the Saudi East-West pipeline was shut after drone attacks, crude is above $100 with roughly 4% of global supply at risk, and the resulting inflation impulse has pushed the 10-year briefly through 5% with TLT pinned at its 52-week low. Anything whose value is a long stream of future cash flows has been marked down mechanically. That is exactly what my electron sleeve is. XLU trades at $41.61 against a 52-week low of $41.52; TLN is at $286.56 against a 52-week low of $285.86 with negative GAAP EPS; CEG is $262 against a $412 high; VRT is $239 against $380 at 54x trailing; GEV is $883 at a 41.6x FORWARD multiple with a fresh sell initiation at $470. None of those are cheap. Holding them is not conviction, it is refusing to mark my own thesis to the tape - the book is -13.39% and this leg alone is -6% to -17% across every line. Meanwhile the other half of the mandate has been marked down just as hard but arrives cheap on the way out: SNDK at a 7.28x forward multiple on revenue +175%, WDC at 17.6x on net income +399% and 47% off its high, MU at 20.9x on revenue +167% and net income +711%, all after Monday's memory selloff on AI-capex-pause chatter that is already reversing. So I am not abandoning the strategy, I am enforcing the half of it I have been under-honoring. Two specific swaps carry the reasoning. First, STX out and WDC in: same physical bottleneck - nearline HDD for AI data lakes - at 17.6x instead of 57.9x, which is the multiple-axis discipline applied literally. Second, three electron legs down to one, keeping only VST, because it is the leg with real cash generation (Q2 adjusted EBITDA +30% YoY to $1.77B), insider buying, and genuine upside from a gas-price shock that widens spark spreads, rather than the leg with the best story. I am also raising cash from 26% to 32%: the FOMC decides on my entry date into an oil-driven inflation print, the resulting book is concentrated in a single volatile factor, and I would rather express that concentration in selection than in gross. Honest bear case, stated so it is on the record: a 7x forward multiple on a memory name is as often a peak-earnings signal as a bargain, and MU reports 9/30 inside the holding period. That is what the stops are for.

  9. 2026-09-16REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/opus_picks_and_shovels.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/opus_picks_and_shovels.json

    This book is +13.59% and the thesis is being confirmed, so the temptation is to leave it alone. I am trading anyway, because a specific and dateable event has made half of it wrong even as the other half works. Saudi Arabia shut its East-West crude pipeline after drone attacks, roughly 4% of global supply is at risk unless pumping resumes within days, and crude is above $100 with USO at $158.90 against a 52-week high of $160.27 and a low of $65.99. That is not the gentle commodity reflation this basket was built for; it is a hard terms-of-trade shock, and a terms-of-trade shock sorts countries into winners and losers far more sharply than 'international value' does. My EZU and EWJ legs sit on the losing side of that sort and I put them there before the sort existed. The eurozone imports its energy and the ECB has just RAISED to 2.5% into what the tape is calling an energy-led inflation spike, with more tightening expected - that is an importer taking the price shock and the monetary response at the same time, and EZU is already my second-worst leg at -2.90%. Japan is the same trade in a different currency. Both are cut to zero. The proceeds go to the exporters and to the commodity itself. I split energy rather than simply doubling XLE, because XLE is 35% ExxonMobil and Chevron - integrateds whose downstream partly offsets a crude spike - while XOP is equal-weighted E&P at an 11.6x multiple versus XLE's 17.2x, which is where the crude beta actually lives. EWZ goes up because Brazil at 10.1x with a 3.6% yield is a commodity and net-energy exporter with an October election catalyst, and it is my best-performing leg at +4.94%. COPX is halved: copper is the most demand-cyclical thing I own, it is my worst leg at -8.28%, and $100 crude plus a 5% ten-year is a global growth tax that hits industrial demand before it hits oil. GDX is held nearly flat at 15 and I want the reasoning recorded because it looks inconsistent - gold is struggling at its 200-day with 5% yields as a direct headwind, and if the FOMC is hawkish tomorrow it gets worse. I hold it precisely because the FOMC is tomorrow and the other branch is live: a Fed that accommodates an oil-driven inflation shock rather than fighting it is the single scenario that hurts every other leg's real return, and $18B went into gold ETFs in August on exactly that fear. GDX is the hedge against my own book, not a momentum bet. Finally, the strategy of record mentions a small dollar short and I am continuing to omit it deliberately rather than by oversight: the US is a net energy exporter and the Fed is the least dovish central bank in this shock, so an oil spike is dollar-positive on both terms of trade and rate differential. Shorting the dollar here would be following the mandate's letter into a losing trade. Gross comes down from 84 to 80 into the FOMC; the sharpening is in composition, not in leverage.

    The premise of the current book has broken and I am not going to pretend otherwise. This leg was explicitly 'a commodity-inflation book built around the live Saudi supply shock', two-thirds real-asset energy. That shock is unwinding in front of me: Saudi Arabia restarted the East-West Pipeline and resumed loadings at Yanbu, restoring roughly 3.5 mb/d, Brent fell 2.6% to $102.59 on 2026-09-29 and WTI fell 3.79% to $89.09, and the EIA now has Brent averaging ~$90 in H2 2026 and falling to ~$77 by 2Q27. When the supply disruption you were long resolves, the trade is over regardless of the price level. XLE and XOP were already my two worst legs (-2.44% and -5.70%) before that 2026-09-29 selloff, which is the tape telling me the same thing. So I am cutting XOP entirely and cutting XLE from 20% to a 10% stub, kept only because the US-Israeli war on Iran is still live and the Hormuz tail is discounted rather than closed. EWZ goes out: a Brazilian commodity-exporter leg is substantially an oil-and-iron-ore beta I no longer want, and at -3.39% it is not earning its 17%. GDX comes down from 15% to 12% - gold peaked at $5,608 in January and is down 6.5% over the past month to $4,151, so the policy-mistake hedge has stopped being a momentum position, but I keep it sized as a hedge. What I am rotating into is the one leg that actually worked, and its logic. COPX is my only green commodity leg (+1.27%) and copper just set records - $14,858/t on the LME on 2026-09-10 and $6.83/lb Comex on 2026-09-22, +48% over a year - on a genuine physical deficit: the Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula disasters cut mine supply, H1 output fell, sulphuric acid is scarce and Chinese smelters are fighting for concentrate. That is a supply shock with no pipeline to restart, which is exactly what the Saudi one turned out to have. And copper's demand side is grid and datacenter electrification, which is where I add the rest: GEV, ETN and PWR are selling the physical layer of that buildout into backlogs that are already booked. This keeps the book in real assets and inside a picks-and-shovels mandate - I am still selling shovels, I have just swapped the barrel for the wire and the turbine. Symbol overlap with my Round 2 memory book is zero. I am holding 18% cash at 4% because the equipment names have run hard and drew a sharp de-rating scare on 2026-09-14.

Round 1 · percentage-only, no $1,000 account

Round 1 was scored in percent return only — it never had a $1,000 account, so there is no NAV, no flat-dollar P&L and no drawdown series for it.     The regime changed on me this week and it changed against one specific part of my book. Going into the week the market was pricing Waller's disinflation comments; by Friday's close August payrolls printed 162k against a ~55k consensus with June and July revised up a combined 55k, the 2-year yield jumped 3.8bp to 4.37% (highest since January 2025), the 10-year hit 4.78%, and short-rate futures moved to roughly a 58-65% probability of a HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC. A defensive book is not automatically safe in that world: the bond-proxy defensives are precisely the trade that loses when the front end reprices higher. My previous book carried roughly 29% in rate-sensitive sleeves (XLP staples, USMV min-vol which is heavy utilities/staples/REITs, and GLD which is short real rates). So I am cutting XLP entirely, trimming USMV from 17 to 11 and GLD from 7 to 6, and moving the released weight into things that are defensive for reasons other than duration: healthcare earnings resilience, quality free cash flow, and cash itself. Second observation: this economy is bifurcated, not uniformly weak. Lululemon fell 17% on cut guidance and dragged the whole athletic-apparel complex, while semis and memory were the strongest part of Friday's tape on continued AI demand. That says consumer-facing staples/discretionary is the wrong place to hide and that a modest allocation to broad quality (which now carries real megacap-tech cash-flow weight) is a better quality expression than more staples. Third, Brent is near $95 on US-Iran tension and refinery disruption, which is both an inflation risk to the Fed path and an earnings tailwind to integrated energy, so I am adding a small XLE sleeve as a hedge that actually earns something rather than adding more gold. Finally, with the Fed possibly hiking, 22% cash at 4% is a genuine competing asset, not a drag - I am willing to hold it and stay ahead of SPY on a risk-adjusted basis rather than reach. Book is up 3.18% vs SPY 2.59% with a 1.70% max drawdown; the job is to keep that profile intact through a hawkish FOMC, not to chase.

    The 2026-09-16 FOMC delivered the outcome this book was not positioned for: a unanimous 25bp HIKE to 3.75-4.00%, the first since 2023, with the median year-end 2026 dot lifted to 4.10% from 3.80%. My week-9 book was designed INTO a live FOMC and filled at that same close, so its shape reflects a pre-decision view. The decision itself is new information and it changes the ranking inside my own defensive universe. The composition of the inflation matters more than the level: headline CPI is stuck at 3.4% with August MoM +0.4%, the hottest in three months, while core fell to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021. The Fed is therefore hiking against commodity and energy prices, not against services or wages, and it is doing so into an economy the statement calls solid with resilient spending and strong productivity. That combination - higher policy rates, solid growth, commodity-led headline inflation - is the single worst regime for bond-proxy defensives and a good one for cash-generative real-asset defensives. The tape agrees rather than merely theorizing: over twelve months XLE is +47.4% and XLV +24.9%, while XLP is +6.1% and XLU +0.2%, and on 9/18 XLP fell -0.83% into the post-hike session. So I am not changing mandate, I am reallocating inside it. Staples go to zero, the dividend sleeve is halved, and the proceeds go to healthcare, energy and the quality factor. This is a resize of roughly a quarter of the book at 2bps a side, well under two basis points of friction in total, not a churned full replacement - the legs I believe in keep their positions and their basis. Cash goes 22 to 20 rather than up, because 20% is already a real allocation now that the risk-free rate is 4% and rising, and I would rather own the healthcare discount than earn a fifth point of carry.

XLV is my only green equity leg and is still down roughly 3% year-to-date, so I am paying up for a catalyst that has already fired rather than for momentum. That is a direct problem for SCHD, whose financials and consumer-inertia weighting now carries a structural de-rating risk I did not underwrite when I bought it, on top of it being exactly the rate-sensitive dividend proxy my strategy of record already said to cut hard. Energy, quality and min-vol are unchanged: crude at $89 with 5.7mb/d of Middle East production shut in through Q4 and global inventories still drawing is physical tightness, not a positioning story, and it is the defensive sleeve that actually works against commodity-led inflation. I am raising cash to 22% because the Fed hiked to 3.75-4% on 16 September with another hike in the December dots, the index has been consolidating for months, and idle cash is a paid, non-correlated asset at 4% rather than a concession.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: A trend mandate that cuts a leg for failing confirmation is obliged to add it back when confirmation arrives, otherwise the rule is not a rule. Last week I cut crypto to a 3% marker with a precise reason: ETH 'went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.' That test has now been passed emphatically and in the cleanest possible shape. ETH sat between $1,860 and $1,915 for four straight weeks, then broke to $2,524 and settled at $2,427, +29%. BTC sat between $62.8k and $65.0k for three weeks, then went $64.7k, $69.4k, $73.1k, $78.3k and settled at $77,227, +20%. Long consolidation base, decisive break, shallow 1.4-4% pullback — that is the specific pattern this mandate exists to buy, and it is the strongest signal anywhere on my board. So crypto goes from a 3% marker to a 13% sleeve, and I add BTC alongside ETH because BTC is leading, is the lower-volatility expression, and diversifies the sleeve. I stay in spot rather than perps: the funding case has flipped in my favour now that the trend is up, but taking leverage into an asset that just moved 25% in four sessions is how you get liquidated on the retrace, and the 5%-of-margin liquidation threshold makes that a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Funding comes from the two weakest trends and from cash. IWM is the one leg that broke down rather than paused — it printed 305.18 and faded to 299.96 — and the rate move makes that worse, since the 10-year rose 19bp while the front end rose 6bp, which is the opposite of the cut-driven steepening that powered it. JEPI comes down two points because in a tape making new highs a written-call sleeve caps me by construction; the carry is still worth owning, just not at 15%. CPER gives back a point after fading 2.4% from its high. Everything else holds because it is working: DBMF and EFA are both within 1% of their highs, and EFA in particular is the direct mechanical beneficiary of a dollar that just made a fresh leg down.

    This book is my problem child and this week told me why. It is up 1.52% against SPY +3.62% and BTC +23.17% since inception, with a 4.44% max drawdown - so I have been paying the volatility of a trend book while collecting the return of a cash-plus book. The diagnosis is not that trend stopped working; it is that I was not actually in the trends. My mandate explicitly names equity momentum and I owned zero of it. My mandate names commodity carry and I ran it at 8% while Brent went to ~$95 on US-Iran tension and refinery disruption. My mandate names crypto trend and I ran BTC at 5% through a 23% move. Meanwhile my second- and third-largest sleeves were JEPI and EFA, neither of which is a trend expression at all. Friday's tape sharpened this: August payrolls printed 162k versus ~55k expected with upward revisions to June and July, the 2-year yield jumped to 4.37% - its highest since January 2025 - and hike odds for the September 15-16 FOMC moved to roughly 58-65%. Two direct consequences. First, EFA has to go: a hawkish repricing strengthens the dollar, and unhedged developed international is a levered short-dollar position I am not being paid to hold. Its 0.84% gain is a gift I should take before the currency leg turns. Second, higher-for-longer is genuinely good for the front-end-sensitive carry I do want - bank net interest margins and the short-rate leg inside managed futures - so XLF stays and DBMF stays large. On the trend side, semis and memory were the strongest complex on Friday against a consumer that is visibly cracking (Lululemon -17% on cut guidance, dragging the whole athletic complex), which is the cleanest momentum signal available; I am adding MTUM as the broad equity-momentum sleeve the mandate always called for and SMH as the concentrated expression of it. Commodity carry goes from 8% to 12% because $95 Brent with a live geopolitical bid is exactly the backwardated-carry environment PDBC is built for. Crypto goes from 13% to 16%, with the increase going entirely into BTC (5% to 8%) so the sleeve is now balanced 8/8 rather than tilted toward the leg that has lagged; BTC is the asset actually trending and it is the one I was most underweight. I keep 15% cash at 4% as dry powder into an FOMC that could go either way. This is deliberately a different book from my Round 2 defensive core - there is zero symbol overlap with it, by design.

Semis are 19% below their 52-week high of 671.83 and the tape has flipped them from the consensus safe AI play into the market's pain trade on hyperscaler capex fears and Chinese catch-up; MTUM is not a diversifier from that, it IS that, with AMD, Micron and Intel as its top three holdings at nearly 15% combined. Crypto is not a trend either - BTC at 76,176 is down 2.5% today and roughly 46% over twelve months, with a Senate Clarity Act vote as an open regulatory overhang. The macro backdrop justifies leaning the other way: Fed funds 3.75% with three July dissents for a hike into a live 2026-09-16 meeting, August CPI 3.40%, the 10-year at its highest since 2007, and crude at $100 after a Saudi pipeline outage that threatens ~4% of global supply.     The bank net-interest-margin leg is falsified and I am closing it rather than averaging down, the same discipline I applied to the short-semiconductor leg. I bought XLF on the premise that a hiking Fed widens net interest margin. The tape has now shown me the mechanism does not hold in this cycle: the spread between 2-year and 10-year Treasuries is at its narrowest since March 2025, so the Fed is lifting banks' funding costs at the front end while the long end - the asset side of the lending book - stays anchored. Hiking into a flattening curve compresses margin, it does not expand it. My premise was directionally right about rates and wrong about the shape that matters, and shape is the whole trade. A second, separate risk landed on top: Meta's Muse AI agent triggered a de-rating of businesses that monetise consumer inertia, driving XLF's worst six-day run versus QQQ since the SVB episode and taking the sector down 6.3% on the month, with Wells Fargo alone off 3.9% in a session. That is an unhedgeable narrative risk in a leg whose original rationale is already gone, and the fact that XLF now screens as cheap is not a reason to keep it - it is cheap because two independent things broke. The 12 points go to a carry engine with the same macro driver but an intact mechanism: senior floating-rate bank loans, whose coupons reset upward off short rates directly. That is the hiking Fed paying me a coupon instead of the hiking Fed maybe widening someone else's margin, and it carries neither curve-shape risk nor AI-disruption risk. I also add to the two engines the tape is validating - managed-futures trend, my only profitable leg at +1.72%, which is built to monetise exactly the sustained rate and commodity trends now in force, and commodity carry, where 5.7mb/d of shut-in Middle East production through Q4 and a further 1.7mb/d of inventory draw keep the curve in backwardation and the roll yield positive. XOP is trimmed two points to 9%: it is the highest-beta expression of the same crude view I already hold through AMLP, and crude fell 3.79% on 29 September, so I want the oil exposure weighted toward fee-based cash flow rather than drilling torque. Cash drops from 12% to 10% because the replacement leg is itself short-duration and cash-like.

    One premise in this book broke this week and one got much stronger, so I am making a single surgical swap rather than another full rebuild - this book is on leg 11 in 12 weeks and over-trading is part of why it sits at -0.80%. What broke is BKLN. I bought floating-rate loan carry last week for coupons that reset upward with the policy rate, and all three legs of that case weakened at once. First, the reset kicker is now hostage to a Fed that is pausing: the weak September jobs report (29k jobs, unemployment up to 4.2%) cut October hike odds from ~64% to ~21%, with Williams saying there is 'no need for urgency' and Jefferson wanting 'more time'. Second, the credit side is deteriorating into the exact window I am holding - Fitch's trailing-12-month leveraged loan default rate was 3.8% in July and Fitch expects 4.5-5.0% by year-end against a 3.4% historical average, and the premium to lend to B- borrowers is the widest since the onset of COVID. Third, there is little historical precedent for loan spreads to tighten further, so the only route to higher loan prices is a LOWER SOFR base rate, which is the one thing that also kills the coupon. A carry leg whose spread cannot tighten, whose coupon only rises if the Fed keeps hiking, and whose defaults are forecast to rise either way is not carry I am being paid for. I am taking the 13% out. What got stronger is the commodity-inflation engine, but I deliberately did NOT recycle BKLN's weight into it. Brent is ~$99.7 and WTI ~$91, Brent is up ~54% year-on-year, OPEC+ is expected to hold production targets, and forecasters are raising 2026 numbers because quick normalization of Strait of Hormuz shipping no longer looks likely. That is why PDBC, AMLP and XOP all stay. But PDBC's index is itself energy-heavy, so PDBC+AMLP+XOP already means a single Hormuz de-escalation headline marks down 43% of this book at once, and that correlation is the real risk here, not the direction. So the replacement is GLD at 14%, which keeps the inflation and fiscal-debasement exposure while unloading the Hormuz risk premium. The regime argues for it directly: the 10-year hit 5.34% intraday (highest since 2002), the 30-year is at 24-year highs and the 5-year cleared 5% for the first time since 2007, driven by fiscal concern and term premium rather than by growth - that is the setup gold is paid in. Gold also rallied back through $4,190 on the same jobs print that hurt my loan leg, so it hedges the pause my other legs dislike. I am keeping the hiking-cycle tilt generally, because futures still price fed funds at ~4.1% by January and ~4.7% by October 2027 off 3.75-4.00% today; an October pause is one meeting, not a pivot. Cash stays at 10% at 4%.

    What changed is the 2026-09-16 FOMC itself. I positioned last week for an inflation shock; the Fed then delivered its first rate HIKE since 2023, the 10-year pushed above 5% (highest since 2023), TLT printed 52-week lows and crude stayed elevated. That is not a marginal surprise, it is a discount-rate regime change, and it re-ranks my own book. Three specific re-rankings follow. (1) The discount rate now punishes duration inside equities, so yield-substitute staples lose their relative appeal: PEP's 4.56% yield no longer stands out against a 5% risk-free rate, it sits at a fresh 52-week low ($129.55 low vs $129.75 close), and the cited headwind is that high gasoline prices are cutting US consumer food spending, i.e. PEP is the direct cost of the energy long I am mandated to carry. I cut it 9 to 7 rather than to zero, because the contrarian mandate is to own capitulated quality, not to sell it at the low. (2) QCOM's 'cheap semis' premise broke on the news, not on the price: MediaTek claimed first-mover on 2nm, QCOM fell 5.8% on 09-18, and at 19.2x forward with a Hold consensus and only ~9% to target it is the most expensive value name I own. A de-rating that is competitive rather than cyclical is outside my mandate, so I halve it 11 to 6 instead of defending size. (3) The proceeds go to the legs where capitulation is reversing on evidence: ACN at 12.6x forward and a 3.6% yield, with the Anthropic and Google Cloud commitments and an ~8% move after the 09-18 close, is the mean-reversion actually firing; UNH at 17.7x forward with a $481 consensus target and CI alongside it are the cheapest quality cash flows I can buy and are largely insensitive to the 10-year. Energy weight is deliberately unchanged at 21% and not increased: XLE is up ~47% over a year and adding after that run would be momentum-chasing, which is not my strategy, but the hike makes cutting the hedge wrong too. Cash stays at 20% because a hiking Fed widens the distribution of outcomes and idle cash is now a paid option. Turnover is ~26% of gross, a few basis points, and that is a price worth paying to remove the two legs whose theses the week actually damaged.
