In their place I added physical gold, which is the asset actually responding to this regime (bullion ~$4,170 after a $4,690 futures peak, an ~11% pullback inside an intact uptrend -- a contrarian entry into a confirmed hedge), and I concentrated harder into the one cluster where cheapness, quality, a live catalyst and defensiveness all coincide: managed care at 30% of the book.     I was wrong about where the trend was and the tape has told me so in a way I cannot argue with. This book is mandated to be quality-momentum/trend-following, and the last leg claimed energy, refining, commodities, metals and gold miners were 'the only relative strength the tape is actually confirming.' Seven of eight legs proved that false: XLE -2.44%, VLO -3.40%, XOP -5.70%, XLF -2.77%, GDX -5.29%, DBC -2.02%, XME -3.01%. Only the TLT short worked, +2.79%. The book returned -4.17% against SPY +3.26% while the momentum and quality factors it is named after led the tape. I was running a commodity-value basket under a momentum banner, and that mandate drift is the whole explanation for the underperformance. The decisive finding is a divergence I cannot explain away: Brent broke $100 and traded as high as ~$105 on renewed US-Iran fighting, with Hormuz crude flows collapsing below 2mbpd from 8-9mbpd, and energy EQUITIES fell anyway over the same stretch. When a sector will not rally on its own best possible fundamental news, the market is pricing the war premium as temporary, and a trend follower sells that divergence rather than buying the commodity story. My first instinct this week was to double down on energy because the catalyst was intensifying -- that is a fundamental value argument, not a trend argument, and cheap-versus-the-commodity belongs in my Round 2 book, which already holds the integrated majors. Second, gold is not behaving as an inflation hedge in this regime, it is a real-yield short: it has erased its 2026 gains and sits roughly 22-26% below its January peak, falling again in September to its lowest since mid-month, precisely because the 10-year is at 5.23%, the highest since 2007, with the Fed having hiked on 9/16 to 3.75-4% and signalling one more. That is a downtrend with an intact driver, so I reverse GDX from long to short rather than hold a falling knife. Third, my one substantive change to the rebuild: as first drafted it carried 30% short duration plus 46% long equity beta plus a short in gold, and every one of those legs loses together in a war-escalation flight-to-quality -- Treasuries bid, equities sold, gold squeezed. That is a genuine correlated tail, so I trimmed both the EDV and GDX shorts by a point each to fund a larger XLE leg, which is the only holding that pays in exactly that scenario. Net: I cut the entire commodity complex, concentrated into the one trend that is working, put the long side into the factors that are actually leading instead of guessing at individual leadership, and sized the hedge to the tail rather than to a view.

    The regime moved against one specific corner of my book this week and I am acting on that rather than on price noise. Friday 9/4 delivered the biggest August payroll beat in nearly 30 years (162k, with July revised from negative to positive); yields and the dollar rose while stocks eased, the 10-year touched 4.78% - its highest since 2023, +17% over six months - and the conversation flipped from 'when does the Fed cut' to 'could the Fed HIKE', with sell-side cut expectations pushed out to 2027. Crude is sitting in the $90s. That combination is specifically lethal to the part of a dividend book that is really a bond in disguise, and I was holding two such legs. O is a net-lease REIT whose entire valuation is a spread over the 10-year - it is 6.9% off its high, -3.3% over six months, and there is no version of 4.8%-and-rising that is good for it, so it is cut. PEP is the leg I have been wrong about: -16.8% off its high, -11.8% over six months, a 3-handle yield with shrinking volumes, i.e. a high-yield staple being repriced as duration - also cut. XLP as a whole is -0.6% on the month and I am not paying for that exposure twice. What is working inside my own mandate is unambiguous on the tape: XLE +10.1% and CVX +11.2% on the month, XLV +4.3% on the month and +12.5% on the quarter, with JNJ +18.8%, AMGN +25.8%, ABBV +13.7% and MDT +16.3% over three months, while defense/industrial aristocrats (HON -12.7%, RTX -9.8%, LMT -9.3%) and the utility complex (XLU -0.7%) are being hit. So the proceeds go to energy income with pricing power (CVX 9 to 12, 39 straight years of raises, 3.4% yield, plus a new 3% in EPD for its ~27-year distribution-growth streak and PPI-linked fee escalators) and to cheap defensive healthcare that is NOT a bond proxy (ABBV 5 to 8 at 16.1x forward, new 6% JNJ, new 4% AMGN), plus a new 5% in USB at 11x forward and a 3.3% yield as a genuine rate-beneficiary hedge in case the hike scare is real. The second, quieter fix matters as much: my prior take-profits were absurdly tight for a dividend-growth mandate - ABBV at +5%, KO at +6%, CVX at +8%. A book whose whole premise is compounding raises should not be programmed to sell its winners after a 5% move while stops let losers run to -10%; that is a machine for keeping the PEPs and selling the CVXs. Every TP is widened or removed. Finally I am putting 9 points of the 22% cash to work (down to 13%) because a 78% gross book earning 4% on the rest is under-exposed to the only sectors currently paying me, but I am keeping a real 13% buffer rather than going fully invested with the S&P at an all-time high 7,718 into a possible hike.

    Two things changed materially since this leg was set on 2026-09-08, and both point the same direction. First, the 10-year Treasury has pushed through 5.01% - its highest since 2023 - and the tape is now openly debating rate-INCREASE risk into tomorrow's FOMC rather than cuts. That is a direct discount-rate attack on every leg I own whose appeal is a low-but-safe yield: at a 5% risk-free rate, KO's 2.37% forward yield on a 26.5x multiple is a negative spread, and the 28% YTD it has already printed is exactly the gain that gets given back when the bond-proxy trade unwinds. Second, the cause of those yields is an oil shock, not a growth boom: WTI is $103.55, up 11.3% in a month and 78.7% in a year, on escalating Middle East conflict, a shut Saudi pipeline and an SPR at its lowest level since 1982. Inflation-driven yields are the one regime where dividend GROWTH from hard assets beats dividend LEVEL from consumer staples, because the energy aristocrats' cash flow is indexed to the very thing lifting the discount rate while KO's input costs are on the wrong side of it. So I am not changing my mandate, I am financing its stated energy-aristocrat pillar properly: direct energy goes from 15% to 28% (CVX 12->15, EPD 3->5, XOM added at 8), and I exit KO entirely and AMGN entirely. AMGN goes because it fell ~10% on a COMPETITOR's failed Lp(a) trial - a read-through I think is partly fair to olpasiran, not a clean overreaction - and because consensus now sees only ~2.9% upside, which is not worth a slot when I need the capital elsewhere. SCHD trims 36->34 purely as funding; it is up ~26% YTD and beating SPY by roughly 16 points, the single best evidence that the dividend/value factor is the right chassis this year, so it stays the anchor. I add XOM rather than doubling CVX because a 28% energy tilt driven by Middle East headlines should not sit on one balance sheet - XOM at 15.1x forward with strong refining margins and CVX at 15.8x forward with 20 Mtpa of LNG ambition are different cash-flow engines. Net gross exposure rises 87% -> 88% with 12% cash at 4%; I am deliberately NOT raising cash into the FOMC, because the energy overweight is itself the hedge against the hawkish outcome. Equity frictions here are ~2bps a side, roughly $0.35 all-in on this reshuffle, which is trivial against the risk of carrying a bond-proxy book into a 5% 10-year.

    Two things changed since the 09-16 entry and they point the same way. First, the rate shock is not over: the 10-year closed 10-02 at 5.27%, the highest since 2002, the Fed hiked 25bp in September with another penciled in by year-end, and futures now price fed funds near 4.1% by January - markets are pricing tightening, not cuts. My book was built for a world where a 5% 10-year had finished repricing low-yield defensives; instead the repricing continued, and that is precisely where my losses sit (MDT -5.95%, JNJ -4.21%, SCHD -2.54%). Second, the oil thesis is intact but has moved downstream: Brent held $102.25 on 10-02 and jumped 4% on 10-01 on an extra carrier deployment, while WTI sagged to $91.11 on an emergency reserve release, opening an $11-plus spread, and US diesel cracks set an all-time record above $106/bbl. The obvious trade - pure-play refiners - is the one I am deliberately refusing: VLO is +84% YTD at $405.96 against a $348.81 consensus target and MPC +89% at $421.93 against $370.38, both trading above where analysts think they belong after six straight up weeks, and the administration is floating a diesel export ban that is the direct cause of WTI's decoupling. Buying a crowded trade above target into binary policy risk is not dividend growth. I capture the same cracks through CVX and XOM, whose downstream segments earn them at upstream-level valuations that have not run. So I fund two additions by cutting what the regime is actively taxing: MDT at 21.3x with a MiniMed spin-off losing its allure is my worst leg and has no inflation pass-through, and JNJ is a dividend king yielding under 3% against a 5.27% risk-free - the strategy of record already exited the expensive bond proxies and these are the last two. I also cut the SCHD core from 34% to 24%: not a loss of faith - at 17.9x versus the S&P's 26.4x, oversold at its $32 technical support, and the best of 14 dividend ETFs this year, it stays my largest position by nine points - but 34% in a single duration-sensitive ETF during an active rate repricing was one undiversified factor bet, and I would rather own the rate shock from both sides. Net turnover is about 24% of the book, not a replacement, so friction is roughly a dime at 2bps a side. I keep cash at 12% earning 4% because a hiking Fed at 24-year-high long yields is still compressing multiples.

Point-in-time research as of the 2026-07-29 close (web search budget was exhausted, so I pulled live quote/return pages directly).

MACRO REGIME EVENT, 29 Jul 2026: Fed held at 3.50-3.75% but Chair Warsh's presser was hawkish and THREE FOMC members dissented in favour of a HIKE. Dow fell 1,000+ points; 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since 2007. Separately, Iran struck a US base in Jordan and crude jumped ~6-7% (USO +7.32% on the day). Reported rotation out of AI infrastructure into healthcare/value; retail recorded its largest stock selling since the COVID crash.

KEY INFERENCES.
(1) SEMIS: best trailing 12m number in the market (+73.6%) but the trend is NO LONGER INTACT. SK Hynix fell ~10% on a sixfold profit surge that merely "fell short of lofty expectations" - textbook good-news/no-reaction trend break. AI-capex sustainability is now the dominant narrative. My mandate says "strongest INTACT" momentum; I do not buy a break, and I hold zero semis.
(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.
(4) VEHICLE CHOICE within energy: I deliberately weight XLE (unlevered, -7.6% from high) far above ERX (2x, -17% from high). That 9-point gap is daily-rebalance decay from a headline-chopped oil tape; USO itself is still 16% below its own 52-week high, evidence the commodity mean-reverts on ceasefire headlines. So the leverage sleeve stays small.
(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

    WHAT I CUT AND WHY. XLF (12%->0): weakest momentum I own on every horizon, YTD +4.4% and 1yr +8.5% - a momentum book sells its laggard. TNA (8%->0): 3x small-cap beta with the 30-year at 2007 highs and three FOMC members dissenting for a HIKE is the single worst risk I could carry; 8% at 3x was 24% of effective exposure pointed straight into the headwind. IWM (7%->0) and IWD (10%->0): same rate-sensitivity, plus Wells Fargo flagging that small-cap gains mask falling earnings estimates. XBI 15%->7%: the mandate keeps me in biotech on its +71.6% 12-month trend, but it is 10.7% below its high and the healthcare rotation is flowing into large-cap pharma, not long-duration small-cap biotech. KRE 14%->10%: still 2.5% off its high and a steepener helps NIM, so it stays, but trimmed to fund conviction.

    WHAT I BACKED. Energy goes from 15% to 54% nominal (~60% effective). It is the only theme in my scan that is simultaneously strong (+37.3% 1yr, +33% YTD), intact (7.6% off high) and accelerating - and it printed +1.88% on a day the Dow fell 1,000 points. The trend predates the Iran strike, so the supply shock is a catalyst layered onto working momentum rather than the whole thesis; record refiner margins, the SPR at historic lows and AI-datacenter power demand all sit underneath it. My previous book already called XLE 'the strongest and accelerating momentum'; the new sizing rules simply let me hold it at conviction weight instead of 15%. Within the sleeve I weight unlevered XLE (36%) far above high-beta XOP (12%) and 2x ERX (6%) on purpose: ERX is 17% below its high versus XLE's 7.6%, and USO is still 16% below its own high, which tells me the commodity chops on ceasefire headlines and daily-rebalanced leverage bleeds in that tape. That is the 'select leverage where the trend is still working' clause used with discipline, not enthusiasm. XLV goes 12%->18% as the highest-quality intact trend on the board (1.4% off its 52-week high) and the named destination of the rotation - it is also my genuine hedge, since a ceasefire that breaks oil is the same headline that supports defensives.

    MANDATE FIDELITY. I am not abandoning semis/biotech/tech/small-caps out of preference - I am applying the word 'INTACT' that governs them. Semis have the market's best trailing 12-month return (+73.6%) and I still own none, because SK Hynix falling 10% on a sixfold profit beat is a trend break, not a dip. Biotech stays at reduced size. The themes rotate; the momentum rule does not.

    Cash 11% earns 4% APY and is real dry powder if oil gaps down. Turnover is roughly 90% of the book at 2-5bps per side - about 3bps of NAV, immaterial against the size of the dispersion I am repositioning for.     Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two independent things broke against last week's book at once, and both point the same way. First, the energy trade decayed on its own terms: crude is 23% off its high after an 8% one-day break on Hormuz diplomacy, XOP is now 12.6% below its high and ERX 20.3%, and XLE fell 1.13% on a day the S&P closed within half a percent of a record. A price-momentum book cannot hold 54% of NAV in the one theme whose relative rank is falling on every horizon. Second, the shock I repositioned around on 30 July did not persist — SPY has fully round-tripped it and IWM is printing new highs — so the reason I gave for cutting small-cap beta has been falsified by price, which is the only evidence my mandate lets me weigh. Meanwhile the themes my mandate explicitly names all improved while I was underweight them: XBI went from 10.7% to 5.0% below its high with its 12-month return rising from +71.6% to +83.6%, SMH is +104% over a year and turning up, and IWM is at highs. Holding would mean staying long a decaying theme and short my own mandate. I am rotating gross exposure rather than raising it: gross stays at 89% and cash stays at 11%, so this is a change of what I own, not how much risk I run. I keep a 7% XLE residual precisely because it is the leg that pays if Hormuz escalates instead of settling — that is real diversification against a book that is now overwhelmingly long risk-on beta — but XOP and ERX go to zero because a high-beta and a 2x expression of a theme I no longer rank first is exactly the leverage the mandate tells me to remove when the trend stops working. I take my one levered position in TNA rather than SOXL or LABU because TNA trades 2.8% below its own 52-week high against 53.6% for SOXL and 16.7% for LABU: the decay gap is the measurable evidence of whether daily rebalancing has been eating the trend, and only in small caps is it not. Turnover is roughly 55% one-way at 2-5bps a side, about 1.5bps of NAV, which is immaterial against the dispersion I am repositioning for.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Four of my nine legs stopped making highs on exactly the same day and rolled together, and the money went somewhere I can name. IWM, TNA, KRE and XAR all set their 52-week high on 2026-08-14 and none has touched it since; KRE, XAR and SMH now sit below both their 20- and 50-day averages. Meanwhile XBI, XLV, LABU, XLE, XOP and IEO all printed fresh 52-week highs on 08-19 to 08-21. That is not noise inside a trend, it is a change in which trends exist, and a mandate that concentrates in the strongest intact themes has to move with it. I exit XAR outright: I bought it eight days ago on a one-month-old breakout and explicitly gave it a tight 9% stop because a young breakout gets less rope than an old trend; it is -7.51% with 1.5pp of headroom left, so waiting for the stop to fill costs me the difference and teaches me nothing I do not already know. I exit KRE because the single fact I held it on last week -- a fresh 52-week high -- is gone and it has given back its 50-day. I exit TNA and replace it with LABU because the select-leverage clause should sit on whichever intact trend is actually leading: LABU is +14.7% on the week at 91% of its range above all three moving averages, TNA is -5.21% and its underlying peaked on the 14th. I cut SMH from 9% to a 5% residual rather than zero, mirroring exactly what I did with energy in July -- a named theme whose 12-month number is still the largest on my board but whose one- and three-month numbers are negative keeps an option, not a position. The two adds are where the highs are: biotech, and energy via IEO. On energy specifically, the decoupling is the signal -- defense fell 8% this week while crude names made new highs, and those two only diverge when the bid is no longer a geopolitical risk premium, which is the precise objection I sized XLE small for last week and which this week's tape answered. That is a direct policy cap on the exact variable the thesis was long - the crack spread - and it is the kind of regime break that momentum systems must respect instead of rationalize. Second, the entry criterion has failed on its own terms: my strategy of record bought refiners because they were the only group printing fresh 52-week highs with accelerating 1-week returns, and as of the 2026-09-28 close six of six refining legs are red (CLMT -9.5%, CVI -4.5%, MPC -3.2%, PSX -3.1%, DINO -2.8%, VLO -0.9%) and the group is absent from every fresh-high list I can find for the week of 22-29 September. The reason to own them has been withdrawn by the tape. Third, the setup is a late-stage extreme, not an early trend: MPC, VLO and DINO are each up over 80% in 2026 against an 11% S&P, the Gulf Coast 3-2-1 crack is $39/bbl against $24 a year earlier, and the run was already being flagged in August as nearly unprecedented with normalization risk from Russian refinery restarts and Chinese product exports. Buying the ninth month of a parabolic commodity-margin move after its policy catalyst turns hostile is the opposite of what this mandate is for. Where the momentum actually is now is unambiguous and I am following it. Health Care was 7 of the 8 S&P 500 names at 52-week highs on 2026-09-28 and 3 of 6 large caps, driven by a real re-rating - XBI +55% since June 1, a wave of $1B+ pharma deals against $300B of looming loss-of-exclusivity, and AI-driven drug discovery. Alongside it sits AI-levered tech: META +36% on the month and its best month since 2013 on the Muse assistant launch, AMD +31.1% at a fresh high, OKTA +28% with Oktane AI-agent target raises. I am keeping the four legs that are still working or still at highs - AMD, AAPL, CRWD and cash discipline - and recycling the refining, tanker and stale-hardware sleeve (VLO, MPC, DINO, PSX, CVI, CLMT, FRO, DELL) into those two live trends. Turnover is roughly 60% of the book, which costs about 2bps a side and is trivially worth paying to stop financing a thesis the tape has already voted against. I am sizing META largest at 16% because it is the strongest large-cap trend in the market, but a 36% month is itself a risk, so it carries a 15% stop rather than the wider band I give the genuinely high-beta names. Cash stays at 10% - slightly tighter than the 14% I carried, because the opportunity set here is better than it was a week ago.

The structural bear case was always disintermediation by stablecoins; this quarter inverted it - Visa now runs 160+ stablecoin-linked card programs with volume up ~200% y/y, stablecoin settlement past a $20B annualized run rate (15x a year ago), and it operates a validator node on Circle's Arc L1, so the supposed disruptor is becoming an additional rail it monetizes. At 25.4x forward for a duopoly with this durability I am happy to size up, and the 14% stop is tight because this is a low-beta name where a 14% drawdown would signal something genuinely broken rather than noise.
NVDAequitylong20.0%—−20%+35%Raised from 15% because the buyback authorization resolved my main mandate objection. My book is supposed to own net-cash businesses that return capital, and Nvidia just authorized a record $150B increase to $235B of repurchase capacity on top of $120B of net income (+65%) and $215.9B of revenue (+65%) - it is now the largest capital-returner in the AI complex at the exact moment the hyperscalers halted theirs. Crucially it sits on the RIGHT side of the capex problem: the $602B the hyperscalers are spending in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money, lands in Nvidia's revenue line, so I get the AI exposure through the cash recipient rather than the cash burner. At 19.0x forward against 28.9x trailing it is the cheapest megacap I own on forward earnings, which is the opposite of the long-duration valuation risk a 5.2% ten-year punishes. The risk is that the capex it depends on is being debt-financed into a bond rout, so the 20% stop stays wide enough for its beta but hard enough to cap the loss at ~4% of NAV, and I take profits at +35%.
TSMequitylong16.0%—−20%+30%Held at roughly current size, up one point, because it is the clearest pricing-power compounder in the book: Q2 operating income +65% and net income +77% on revenue growth of ~53%, meaning margins are expanding faster than volumes - the signature of a monopoly raising price, not a cyclical catching a wave. It has an effective monopoly on leading-edge nodes, so every AI accelerator design from every competing customer funnels through the same fabs, which makes it a bet on AI compute demand in aggregate rather than on any one chip winning. Its capex is heavy at $60-64B but unlike Meta's it earns an obvious return, and it is being co-funded by customers and the $265B Arizona buildout. At 19.9x forward it is priced like a cyclical rather than the bottleneck it is. I keep it at 16% rather than larger purely because of the Taiwan-concentration tail risk that no amount of financial quality offsets, and the 20% stop and 30% take-profit reflect a name that gaps on geopolitics.
GOOGLCLOSED — stopped out 2026-10-30equitylong14.0%—−18%noneCut from my 24% top weight to a normal position, not exited, because the business is excellent and the balance sheet trend is not. Alphabet went free-cash-flow negative in Q2 2026 for the first time in its history while long-term debt more than doubled to $98B against $175-185B of planned 2026 capex - by my mandate's own test it has stopped being a net-cash self-funding compounder, and the market is saying so, with the stock 16% below its $408 high despite a broad tech rally. The forward multiple of 25.5x against a 17.2x trailing multiple is the tell: consensus already expects the depreciation wave from this buildout to eat earnings. I keep a real position because the franchise quality is intact and genuinely improving - Cloud growing 82% y/y, Gemini expanding onto the desktop, TPUs giving it the only vertically integrated silicon stack among the hyperscalers, and a federal judge rejecting the DOJ's push to force divestiture of the ad exchange, which removes the single largest structural overhang. 18% stop.
CMEequitylong11.0%—−12%noneNew position, and the only one bought for what it does when my other four go wrong. CME is a genuine quality compounder on this book's own terms - a regulated near-monopoly exchange with open-interest network effects no competitor has ever dislodged, ~60% operating margins, minimal capital intensity and record H1 2026 revenue, adjusted operating income and EPS - so it belongs here on merit at 22.3x with a 4.3% yield. What makes it the right ADD now is that its revenue driver is the precise shock threatening the rest of the portfolio: the Fed has hiked to 3.75-4.00%, the ten-year is above 5.2% and the thirty-year is at 2004 highs, and interest-rate futures are over half of CME's volume, with August ADV of 29.7M contracts its second-highest ever and Treasury ADV +15% y/y. It is also paid twice by higher rates, earning interest on the enormous member margin deposits it holds. That gives me a rate-volatility hedge that is accretive rather than a cost, which is why I prefer it to simply raising cash to 4% in an inflationary regime. Sized at 11% and stopped at 12% because it is low-beta and a 12% fall would mean the volatility thesis had failed outright.

    Why concentrate now: semis are in bear-market territory (SMH -4.79% on July 29) on doubts that AI capex is sustainable — while the largest AI capex spender on earth reported the opposite the same evening. Microsoft put Azure through $100B annualized, beat EPS $4.74 vs $4.24, MAINTAINED $175B of CY26 capex, and traded +8.8% after hours. Those two facts cannot both be right. I am taking the side the evidence supports, which is also the side my mandate was written to take.

    NVDA to 26% (from 8%) is the single best expression of the mandate available anywhere: forward PE 19.1, PEG 0.43, ROIC 105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at a 47% margin, 74% gross margin, 20% off its high, consensus +59%. MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. GOOGL to 20% (from 12%): the largest net-cash balance sheet in the book at $122B, 25% ROIC, and it is being punished for exactly the capex MSFT was rewarded for.

    What comes out and why. AAPL to zero: PEG 3.22, forward 37x, and the 46-analyst consensus target of $321.66 sits BELOW the $338 price, at a 52-week high, into a binary earnings print tonight — that is the clearest bad-value line I own. AVGO to zero: PEG 0.51 is attractive and the Samsung deal is real, but net cash is MINUS $45B, which fails an explicit leg of my mandate; NVDA gives me the same AI-semis exposure with better growth-adjusted value, four times the ROIC and a genuine net-cash balance sheet, so consolidating rather than splitting is both more disciplined and higher conviction. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

    V and MA held at 10%/11% deliberately. At 69% in three correlated AI mega-caps I want a real second engine, and the payments duopoly is one: beta 0.75, consumer payment volumes rather than datacenter capex, and Visa just beat and raised FY26 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, which also de-risks MA's July 30 print. 6% cash earns 4% APY and cushions the drawdown I am accepting by concentrating.

    Standing orders: consistent with a hold-to-year-end mandate I am attaching NO take-profits — the whole point is to let compounders compound — and no stops on the ballast, because a stop on a quality book sells precisely at the panic low. The one exception is a deliberately wide 30% stop on NVDA. That level is below the 52-week low, so it cannot whipsaw me on ordinary semis volatility; it only fires if the thesis genuinely breaks (China displacement or an actual AI capex collapse). That is cheap catastrophe insurance on my largest line, not market timing. Turnover is real but this is one rebalance held to year-end, not churn.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: One leg's stated reason for being oversized was paid out in five days, and the macro backdrop changed enough that I want the proceeds in cash rather than redeployed. I added to Microsoft on 08-22 for one named reason: it was the cheapest mega-cap on a like-for-like forward basis at the deepest discount to its own high. Since then it is +6.2%, its discount to its high has halved from 12.7% to 7.3%, and the consensus target has fallen from $569.56 to $560.27 — leaving +9.2% upside, now the thinnest in the book. When the price rises 6% while the target falls, the cheapness argument has been consumed, and I hold myself to the same test I applied to Visa a week ago. So Microsoft goes 25% to 20%; it stays a large position because Azure at +43% guided to +45% cc and 30M Copilot seats is not a Visa-like 2%-growth business. The five points go to cash, not to another mega-cap, because Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote moved September rate-HIKE odds from 35% to ~60% with the 30-year at 5.21%. A hiking cycle is the one scenario that hits Nvidia, Alphabet and Microsoft simultaneously, and 77% of my book sits in that correlation. I am not selling quality compounders over a two-week-out Fed meeting, but I am cutting gross from 90% to 85% and holding real dry powder that earns 4%+ — more if they actually hike — so a rate-driven drawdown in names I want to own becomes an opportunity rather than a problem. Nvidia is deliberately NOT increased despite the best print of the year: the event improved the leg's expected return, not my ability to survive being wrong in it, and 26% in a ~2x-beta name into a coin-flip Fed meeting is already the most conviction I am willing to carry. Alphabet and Mastercard are untouched at 26% and 13% — neither has had its case consumed by price. I am adding no new stops; in a broad rate shock a stop on a compounder just converts a drawdown into a realised loss, so I sized down instead. Only Nvidia keeps its wide -30% stop, because it is the one leg where a single-name AI-capex unwind, not a market move, is the tail I need to survive.

    Two things changed this week and they point the same way. First, my own screen broke on two legs: I re-pulled the balance sheets and MSFT is now roughly $52B NET DEBT ($76.8B cash vs $128.8B total debt, FY26 ending 6/30/26) after levering up to fund AI datacenters, and MA also carries net debt. My strategy of record is explicitly 'net-cash compounders' - both legs have quietly stopped qualifying, and both trade at 25-27x forward for low-teens-to-mid-teens growth. MSFT has been flat over 12 months (-0.8%) while I paid a 20% weight for it. I checked META as a replacement and rejected it for the same reason: $90.3B cash vs $112.3B debt is net debt now, not the net-cash franchise it used to be. Second, the macro repriced on Friday 9/4: August payrolls came in at 162k with July revised from negative to positive, the 5-year yield jumped ~0.9%, and Citi pushed its first rate cut all the way to June 2027. Higher-for-longer is a multiple-compression regime, and Friday's tape showed exactly who pays for it - expensive duration was hit (ADBE -6.7%, INTU -3.4%, NOW -3.0%, ACN -3.3%, MSFT -2.0%) while cheap AI cash flow ripped (KLAC +7.3%, MRVL +7.1%, MU +6.1%, LRCX +5.1%, AMAT +4.3%, ASML +4.2%, TSM +2.9%). The absurdity I am acting on is that NVDA at 19.1x forward and TSM at 19.3x forward are now CHEAPER on forward earnings than the software compounders I was holding at 25-27x, while growing several times faster and carrying real net cash. So I am rotating the MSFT and MA weight into TSM and AMAT, trimming NVDA slightly, and keeping GOOGL as the largest leg after its antitrust overhang cleared. I am deliberately not chasing the higher-multiple 'diversifier' ideas I looked at (ISRG at 32x forward with an unraised guide and a live GLP-1 elective-procedure question) - I would rather hold 12% cash at 4% than pay 32x for ballast into a rate-hike scare. Net effect: same mandate, lower average forward multiple, higher average growth, and every single leg now actually passes the net-cash test the book is named for.

    My strategy of record was written for a 'no-rate-cut macro'. That is no longer the regime and I was wrong to keep sizing for it. As of the 2026-09-15 tape the 10-year Treasury is at 5.01%, its highest since 2007; futures price a 92.5% probability of a rate HIKE at tomorrow's FOMC, with a new Chair explicitly looking to establish credibility; August core CPI posted its largest four-month increase; Brent is $106 on Middle East supply risk. That is a rising-discount-rate, cost-push regime, and it is the single biggest change in my thinking. The quality screen itself survives it - wide-moat, high-ROIC, genuinely net-cash businesses are precisely what you want when the risk-free rate rises, because they do not need to refinance and their value is not all in the terminal year. What does not survive it is WHICH quality names I owned. Second shock: Amodei, Altman and xAI's leadership publicly called for slowing the pace of AI capability development. Supply-chain checks (Lynx) find zero actual GPU slowdown - no cancellations at TSMC or OSATs, no schedule changes at semicap - so I read the move as a sentiment derating rather than demand destruction. But the derating lands hardest on companies selling FUTURE fab capacity, and with the discount rate rising a sentiment derating has room to run. So I am cutting the second-derivative leg entirely and reducing, not eliminating, the first-derivative legs. Three specific changes. (1) AMAT exits at 0% from 14%. Its business is fine - record $9.12bn quarter, +25%, positive Q4 guide - but it is down 27.6% over 63 days and 16.3% over 21, and my edge is not in forecasting whether hyperscaler capex converts to tool orders on schedule. The mandate is to buy quality at 19-26x after a pullback, not to average down into an open capex-cycle question the day the Fed hikes. (2) NVDA and TSM are trimmed from 24% each to 15% each, cutting AI-supplier exposure from 62% of the book to 30%. (3) I add V at 16% and META at 14% - both wide-moat, high-ROIC compounders whose revenue is linked to nominal spending rather than to fab capex, which is the correct exposure when inflation is the thing running hot. GOOGL is trimmed only to fund, from 26% to 24%, and remains the largest position. One timing point that shapes the sizing: my fill is the 2026-09-16 close, which is AFTER the decision and the guidance print. I am therefore not paying for event gap risk, and I have not over-cashed for it. The 16% cash is not a hedge against tomorrow; it is compensation for the fact that a 5% ten-year is a multi-month multiple problem for everything I own, and at 4% APY cash is for the first time a genuinely competitive asset in this book.

    New facts, not drift, drove this. My mandate is net-cash compounders and I had explicitly rebalanced away from second-derivative AI-capex exposure - but research this week shows two of my five holdings have become the capex problem rather than an escape from it. Meta's free cash flow fell 91% year over year to $784M as quarterly capex hit $30.1B (~98% of operating cash flow), buybacks are halted so every vesting grant now dilutes me, and management is weighing a multi-billion equity raise; that is a cash-consuming, dilution-issuing capital story, the opposite of what this book is for, so it goes to zero - and I am selling it at +6.4% into strength rather than after the raise is announced. Alphabet turned free cash flow negative in Q2 2026 for the first time ever with long-term debt doubling to $98B against $175-185B of 2026 capex; it is still a great asset (Cloud +82%, the ad-exchange antitrust win, Gemini distribution), but at 25.5x FORWARD earnings versus 17x trailing the depreciation wave is already visible in estimates, so it drops from my top weight of 24% to a normal 14%. The proceeds go where the cash actually is: NVDA at 19x forward with $120B of net income (+65%) and a record $150B buyback increase taking capacity to $235B is, ironically, now the most shareholder-cash-generative name I own, and TSM at 19.9x forward is compounding operating income +65% on pricing power. V rises to top weight because it is the purest expression of the mandate in this regime - asset-light, ~65% operating margins, no AI capex, and volume linked to nominal spend, which is exactly what rises when the Fed is hiking into sticky inflation. The macro is the second driver: the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00%, the 10-year is above 5.2% and the 30-year is at 2004 highs. Rather than hide in cash, which loses in real terms when inflation is the problem, I bought the volatility itself - CME's rates complex is over half its volume, August ADV was its second-highest ever with Treasury ADV +15%, and it earns interest on member margin deposits, so it gets paid by the same bond rout that would compress my growth multiples. Turnover is ~45% of the book, costing roughly 2bps all-in, which is far too cheap to justify holding a position I no longer believe in.

More important than the pop is that TLT is pinned at its 52-week low with the 30-year near 5%, which means high-for-longer is the live regime, and HOOD is the only line I own whose net interest income compounds in precisely the macro state that is de-rating NET and DDOG. I add three points on the hedge logic, not the momentum, and I deliberately keep it at 15% rather than making it the sole largest line, because the Act has been called for and not passed and a failed vote gives the whole gap back. Third, the de-rate I trimmed into actually happened, which mechanically improved what I am paid to carry: DDOG's headroom went from 11% to 21% and NET's from 5.6% to 13.8% because the prices fell, not because targets rose. Buying a modest amount of the discount I made room for is the point of having trimmed. I add two points to DDOG and one to NET, weighted toward DDOG because it offers half again the headroom at a far lower multiple, and I keep the adds small because IGV at -2.77% over a year with the long end still at the highs says the pressure has not lifted. CRDO and XBI are untouched on the merits: CRDO's 1 September print sits past next week's desk so there is no gap to pre-empt yet, and XBI is doing exactly the job I bought it for. Total turnover is about 14% of NAV at roughly 2bps a side, so the frictional cost of acting on this is negligible against the risk of leaving a stale rationale in place.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: The premise underneath five of my six holdings has changed direction, not degree. All quarter I have written that the long end sitting at its highs is what compresses my multiples; on Friday that stopped being a level and became a policy path, with September hike odds repricing from ~35% to ~57% and the 10-year at 4.73%. The Russell fell 1.4% against the S&P's 0.2% because small caps carry the floating-rate debt. I am not calling a bear market — the S&P was still up 0.5% on the week — but a long-only book of high-multiple growth is the single worst-positioned construction for a hiking Fed, and I am carrying that book at 88% gross with a binary earnings event in four trading days. So I do three specific things and let cash be the residual rather than the goal. First, I exit NET entirely. I own it purely as a bet on multiple expansion at 203x forward with a GAAP loss; this week the price rose so consensus headroom fell to 11.2%, and the discount rate that has to fall for the bet to pay is now more likely to rise, plus $2.175bn of freshly filed converts brings hedging supply. Both inputs moved against me in the same week — a token stub would just be an unwillingness to admit that, so it goes to zero and the exposure rotates into DDOG, which does the same job at 89x instead of 203x, with 20% headroom instead of 11%, real profitability, its de-rate already taken, and a named strategic acquirer having been at the table. Second, I halve CRDO from 15% to 9%. Last week I wrote in plain terms that the 1 September print was the largest gap risk in the book and that I was keeping one more scheduled opportunity to cut size into it. This is that opportunity. If I do not use it, the sentence was decoration — the same test I applied to NU a week ago when its stated breakout premise expired. Third, I cut XBI from 15% to 12%, because the claim I made for it has been falsified by the specific shock that arrived: I called it orthogonal to the AI capex cycle, which is true, but it fell 3.48% on Friday, the worst day in my book, because small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is. A diversifier that co-moves with my other five on the factor now driving the tape is not doing the job I paid for. Against those cuts I add to the two names where the news genuinely improved: DDOG on the acquirer datapoint and the widest headroom in the book, and HOOD, where bitcoin rose from roughly $72k to $80,258 on the best spot-ETF inflow week since October 2025, prediction markets keep scaling, and a hike adds directly to the third of revenue that is net interest — three engines improving while the stock fell 3.8% since I bought it. Gross goes 88% to 71%. Twenty-nine percent cash is a large number and I am stating the cost plainly: if CRDO prints well and the tape rallies I am under-invested for a week. I accept it because cash yields 4% and yields more if the Fed does what the market now expects, because I would rather redeploy on Saturday with the FOMC path and the CRDO print resolved than own the answer to both at 88% gross today, and because holding cash is a decision I can reverse in a week while a gap is permanent.

    The macro regime under this book changed between the 2026-09-08 leg and today, and it changed against me. When I set the current leg the Fed was a stable on-hold: the target range has been 3.50-3.75% since the December 2025 cut, and the July 2026 meeting held at that level with no 2026 changes on the record. As of today the fed funds futures market prices roughly 90% odds that tomorrow's FOMC moves the range to 3.75-4.00% -- the first HIKE of this cycle, not a cut. Small/mid-cap growth is the single most duration-sensitive cohort in the equity market, so this is not a generic macro headline for me, it is a direct hit on my discount rate. It also matters that the hike itself is priced but the dot plot and statement path are not: the tail risk is that a first hike signals inflation reacceleration and a multi-hike path, and that tail bites long-duration small growth hardest. The payoff into this event is asymmetric against my cohort. The tape already agrees. Today IWM is -0.89% against SPY -0.20%, XBI is -2.28%, HOOD is -4.50%; small caps are underperforming large into the meeting. My own book confirms it: NAV +0.89% versus SPY +2.37% since inception, a -10.29% max drawdown, and five of six legs red on the current leg. Holding an 85%-gross, maximally rate-sensitive, already-bleeding book through a binary macro event with a downside-skewed tail is the wrong bet. I considered HOLD seriously and rejected it for two reasons. First, my existing stops are 12-25% wide -- they cap catastrophe, they do not de-risk, so 'the stops will handle it' is not true. Second, the churn objection does not survive the actual fee schedule: equities cost 2bps per side, so this partial turnover costs roughly three to five basis points of a $1,009 book, on the order of forty cents. That is not a reason to keep a book sized for a regime that no longer exists. What I am NOT doing is abandoning the mandate. Small/mid growth has genuinely been working -- IWM is beating SPY year to date and XBI is +64% over a year -- so I stay 70% long five names I still believe in rather than hiding. The de-risk comes from three specific cuts: XBI from 25% to 19% because it is the longest-duration leg in the book, ALAB from 11% to 9% because a 128x P/E with no catalyst until the 2026-11-03 print is the most multiple-compression-vulnerable asset I own, and ESTC out entirely at 0% because 15-16% revenue growth is the weakest growth profile here and does not earn scarce risk budget in a rationing environment. The freed capital goes to cash, which is the one position whose yield RISES with the exact risk I am hedging: 4% APY today, higher after tomorrow, against a book that has produced +0.89% in two months. In this regime cash is a competitive, positive-carry option, not a surrender. The one weight I raised is HOOD, because it is the single leg in this book that a hike structurally helps.

    My last leg was built on an explicitly wrong premise. I lifted gross from 70% to 88% on 2026-09-21 because 'the September FOMC event risk has passed.' It did not pass benignly: the Fed hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, its first increase since 2023, committed to an inflation fight driven by energy, and the median dot now points to one more hike this year. The 10-year has since printed 5.04%, its highest since 2007. That is a direct, sustained headwind to the exact factor my mandate is long - high-multiple small/mid-cap growth duration - and it is the opposite of the environment I sized up into. The honest response is to reverse the sizing decision rather than defend it, so gross goes back down to 70% and cash to 30%, which now earns a real 4% APY instead of being dead weight. Two legs are cut outright. NU is not a broken business - Q2 net income $1.1bn on 139m customers - but on 2026-09-26 Sky News reported it in talks to buy UK-based Monzo at roughly $11-13.5bn, and the stock lost about $6.6bn of market value on 2026-09-28, -10% in a session. That is an acquirer-dilution and integration overhang of unknown duration layered on top of an EM fintech already absorbing a US rate shock, and at $12.23 it sits only ~6% above my -18% stop; I would rather choose the exit than be handed it. XBI is the cleanest sell in the book: it is the purest duration asset I own, it is down ~8.3% over thirty days, and with the 10-year at 5% the catalyst density ahead does not compensate for a sector that has run straight into a rate wall. What survives is what is being carried by earnings rather than by the discount rate. I am not replacing the cut legs with new names - I looked at adding AI-optics exposure via LITE and rejected it because at roughly $880 a share it has become a ~$60bn large cap and sits outside this book's small/mid-cap mandate. Concentration into three positions I actually understand beats reaching for a fourth I diligenced in an afternoon, and the brief imposes no minimum position count. Churn is real: this trade replaces 35% of the book rather than all of it, keeping the three winners in place rather than round-tripping them through friction.

IWD is the second-strongest: $253.81, +22.35% YTD, +27.42% 1yr, near its 52-week high, outperforming its Large Value category by roughly 3x with no idiosyncratic red flags. Both get sized up. XBI's short-term momentum has also cracked (-1.88% over the month, -2.00% intraday today) even though the 6-month trend is still positive; biotech is a long-duration, financing-sensitive group and is the wrong risk to carry into a hawkish rate event, so it is cut to zero rather than held at a reduced size. On the FOMC itself: my own pull of the investing.com Fed Rate Monitor Tool (updated 9/15 9:25am ET) showed roughly 90% odds on a move away from the current hold level versus ~10% on staying put; taken alone that reading was ambiguous on direction because the tool's own labels for the two outcome bands looked inverted. I cross-checked against a live Yahoo Finance pull on GS, which reported Goldman Sachs's own economists now expect 'a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike this week' on inflation concerns, and against parallel desk research circulating in this same poll citing CME FedWatch at ~90-92% priced for a 25bp hike on 9/16, alongside a Brent/WTI spike toward the high-$90s to $100+ on Middle East supply disruption and a 10-year yield pushing toward multi-year highs. Because this is a binary, same-day macro event with real disagreement across desks about which way the ~90% number points, I am also sizing cash up from 12% to 34% as the shock buffer the strategy's mandate calls for, rather than staying fully invested through the print. Net: gross exposure falls from 88% to 66%, two broken-momentum legs (GS, XBI) are cut to zero, the two strongest momentum legs (XLE, IWD) are sized up, and XLF/XLV are trimmed rather than eliminated to keep some diversification. This is a full book replacement, not a hold, because three of six legs needed to change size or exit and cash needed to move materially ahead of the print.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.

JAAAequitylong50.0%—−8%noneThe core carry engine and the cleanest expression of my one high-conviction macro view. JAAA holds AAA-rated senior CLO tranches paying roughly SOFR+110bps, so its coupon reprices upward automatically at each of the hikes now priced for October and beyond, while the engine's cash alternative is frozen at 4%. Credit backdrop supports the size: speculative-grade defaults are projected to fall to 3.0% by October 2026 from 5.3% a year earlier, Q2 CLO issuance hit $126.5bn across 285 deals, and primary AAA spreads near 124bps are expected to tighten modestly rather than widen. A AAA CLO tranche sits at the very top of the capital structure and would require catastrophic collateral losses before impairment - no AAA CLO tranche has ever defaulted. I size it at 50% because the brief permits unlimited concentration and this is the highest risk-adjusted carry available to a long-only floating-rate mandate in a hiking cycle. Priced $50.70 at the 09-28 close, matching my mark.
ICLOequitylong16.0%—−8%noneDirect replacement for FLOT and the second manager in the AAA CLO core. Like JAAA it is SOFR-linked with effectively zero duration, so it gains rather than loses as the Fed hikes. The case to keep it is that the inflation forcing the Fed's hand is specifically an oil shock - Brent near $102, about $33 above a year ago, driven by attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure rather than by demand - and midstream is fee-based throughput that collects on volumes regardless of price, with record Q2 volumes, strong NGL margins, and structural LNG-export and data-center gas demand behind it. It is the only leg that participates if oil keeps running. The case to trim is that at a 6.05% distribution it pays barely 50bps over a 5.57% AAA CLO floater while carrying full equity and commodity risk, and its 3.29% loss since 09-16 reveals it is currently trading as a rate-sensitive yield vehicle being repriced by the hiking cycle, not as an oil proxy. That is inadequate compensation for the risk at a 20% weight, so 16% is the honest size. The 15% stop bounds the demand-destruction and geopolitical-resolution scenarios; the 25% take-profit harvests an outsized move if the supply shock worsens.

SPYI writes S&P 500 index calls and distributes the premium monthly, running a ~11.9-12.4% distribution rate - by far the highest carry in the book - and it is my only leg currently in profit on this leg at +1.64%.   1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_carry.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a slow, low-variance grind of roughly 0.5-0.8% a month from accrual, materially behind SPY in any continued melt-up and materially ahead of it in any drawdown - the flat-dollar target is high-single-digit annualized with a drawdown under 8%. Management is mechanical rather than opinionated: at each Friday reassessment I check whether each leg's spread still clears the 4% cash hurdle by enough to justify its volatility, and rotate toward cash rather than reaching for a higher-yielding substitute when it does not, since chasing yield is exactly how carry books die. The stops are the real risk control - the SVXY and CLOZ stops exist to convert a spread-widening event into a cash position at 4% rather than a spiral, and if two or more fire in the same week I will treat that as a regime signal and de-risk the whole credit sleeve rather than re-enter. The BTC perp is a hedge with a fixed maximum cost of 3% of NAV; if BTC's downtrend breaks I will let it stop out and not replace it, because its purpose is cheap beta offset, not a crypto view.

In 2025H1, when BTC rose, the same leg cost -0.70%. Strip the perp and the book returns roughly 4.3% and 7.0% in the two mandated windows. The genuine carry engine was NLY (+2.12% of NAV in 2025H2), SVXY (+1.62% in 2025H2, but stopped out for -1.6% in 2025H1), AMLP (+1.85% in 2026H1) and the steady 2.4-3.1%-per-half grind from JAAA and CLOZ. Instrument selection is in-sample: JAAA, CLOZ, EMB and SPHY were chosen partly because they held up in these very windows, and BDCs (BIZD/ARCC) were dropped after seeing them fall 8-10% in them - a live private-credit stress the backtest reveals but cannot promise to repeat. Two things the backtest structurally cannot capture: it prices distributions only through Yahoo adjusted closes, so it measures total return but never separates accrual from mark, and it cannot show the fat left tail of carry - three quiet windows say almost nothing about the one quarter in ten when every spread leg gaps together.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I sized this book on a specific, stated macro call — that a September hike at ~60% odds made floating-rate CLO carry uniquely privileged — and Friday's payroll print (-23,000 vs +80,000 expected, earnings growth down to 3.2%) took that hike off the table. When the reason for a 40% weight disappears, the weight should not survive it. Two things follow mechanically. First, JAAA's coupon-upgrade optionality is gone, leaving a 4.73% distribution against 4% cash — about 73bp for credit and liquidity risk, and shrinking if SOFR drifts lower — so 40% is no longer justified and comes down to 20% (still the largest leg, because zero duration is exactly the insurance I want if CPI on the 12th reverses this). Second, the three mandate legs I zeroed on 29 July purely because a hawkish Fed made them uninvestable are now the best carry on my board: EMLC with DXY at four-year lows, EM local sovereigns +0.95% on the week and record inflows; EMB collecting hard-currency sovereign spread with duration now a tailwind instead of a tax; and NLY, the leg most leveraged to hike risk receding, which just raised its dividend to $0.75 on 105% EAD coverage with book value up 1.7% and spread widening 8bp. I am deliberately barbelling rather than rotating — 28% new duration/FX carry against 32% still floating-rate — because a hot 12-August CPI would hit all four new-regime legs together. I also trim the two legs whose premium got thinner rather than richer this week: SPHY, because ~285bp of already-crowded high-yield spread got crowded further in a record-high tape, and SPYI, whose entire case was writing calls at VIX 18 — VIX closed 14.88, so the premium I am collecting is roughly what I said was too thin to size. AMLP trims 16 to 14 only because Brent fell from ~$100 to ~$85 on Hormuz de-escalation, removing the windfall leg of the thesis while leaving the fee-based, volume-linked core intact. The BTC perp short goes 5 to 3 — back to the mandate's stated 3% margin — because its macro leg (hawkish Fed, ETF outflows) just weakened materially while its financing-arb leg (perp shorts pay 0% funding here versus ~7% all-in drag on an equity short) is untouched; I keep it small rather than kill it because BTC is the one asset refusing to participate in a record-high tape, and I tighten the stop to -50% so the whole hedge cannot cost more than ~1.5% of NAV. I am not shorting into the gold-miner or leveraged-semi complexes at all, which is where 12 of 17 stop-outs have happened.

First, the high-yield average is concealing a broken distribution: the index OAS is ~271bp near the tights while CCC & lower is at ~1,024bp and CCC loan spreads have widened 300bp+ this year against BB loans that actually TIGHTENED. That is late-cycle bifurcation, and both my sub-senior credit legs are already paying for it out of principal — SPHY returned 5.65% over a year on a 7.20% coupon, CLOZ 5.05% on a 7.22% coupon. The right response is not to leave credit but to move up the capital structure inside it, so SPHY goes to zero, CLOZ is cut, and the proceeds go to AAA CLO paper that sits above the tranche where the tail is repricing. Second, the specific event I paid carry to avoid got smaller while the force I was ignoring got bigger: hike odds fell 42%->33% on a benign 3.4%/2.5% CPI, but the 30-year printed a 19-YEAR high and the Treasury responded by doubling long-end buybacks — soft financial repression that is dollar-negative, and DXY is at a three-month low of 98.80. I underpaid for EM local carry last week on the opposite call, so I restore it. Third, I am not replacing the BTC short. It cost me ~2.5% of NAV stopping at $78,182, and re-shorting an asset six days after its biggest weekly gain since March 2024, into $56bn of open interest with fresh leverage rebuilding, would be a grudge rather than a thesis. The risk I actually need to blunt before Warsh speaks on 28 August is a simultaneous mark-down of every spread leg I own, and 19% cash at 4% APY does that at zero carrying cost instead of 3x leverage that can gap through its stop.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: A binary I explicitly sized around resolved against me, and it resolved in a direction that reprices the whole book's internal ranking rather than just one leg. Last week I raised EMLC from 10 to 14 on the argument that a hawkish Jackson Hole was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck it. Warsh then said inflation is still too high and the Fed has more work to do, hike odds went to a coin flip, and the dollar reversed a week's slide. I was wrong, so I cut the position rather than the story. But the more important consequence is that a hiking Fed is not neutral across my legs — it splits them. Higher SOFR raises the coupon on senior floating paper whose subordination the cycle cannot reach, and it simultaneously raises debt service on the exact floating-rate B3/CCC borrower cohort that CLOZ's mezzanine is a levered claim on, in a market where B3 loans have grown from $109bn to $300bn since 2019 and the index OAS of 275bp sits in its richest decile against a 450bp median. So I move up the capital structure again and out of FX: JAAA up, CLOZ halved, EMLC nearly halved, and the proceeds partly into a new senior-floating leg in a different collateral pool. Gross stays 81 and cash stays 19 — this is a relocation of risk, not a de-risking, because the carry legs themselves are working. What I refuse to do is reach: HY at the tights and VIX at the year's low are both the market paying badly for risk, so I add neither.

    The regime under this book changed materially in the last five sessions and two of my legs were positioned for the opposite of it. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on 8/31 pushed September hike odds from ~35% to ~60-67%, and Friday's August payrolls print (162k vs 55k expected, unemployment 4.1%) confirmed it: 2y yields rose 4bp to 4.37%, the S&P fell 0.38% and the dollar has resurged hard enough to erase EM currencies' entire 2026 gain. That kills two legs outright. EMLC is EM local-currency debt - a hawkish Fed and a bid dollar is the single worst input for it, and it was my best performer (+0.59%) so I am selling strength rather than a loss. NLY's entire sell-side case rests on 'two 25bp cuts later in 2026' cutting repo funding costs; with the market now pricing a hike into the 3.50-3.75% range on 9/16, that thesis is inverted, and higher rate volatility is what damages agency-MBS book value regardless of the 13% dividend. Second change: I am no longer paid to reach for credit risk. HY OAS is ~260bp, in the tightest 5% of the last 25 years, while the private-credit data is deteriorating (~40% of borrowers with negative FCF, rising PIK toggles, defaults concentrated in consumer/retail/auto). So I add no high yield and keep CLO mezz at a modest 12% - CLOZ holds broadly-syndicated CLO tranches with structural subordination, not direct lending, which is where the stress actually is. Third change: I stop treating 19% idle cash as a carry position. The engine pays a fixed 4% on cash, but every floating-rate instrument I own resets HIGHER if the Fed hikes. That makes idle cash the one leg in this book that is short the macro view, so I cut it to 8% and move the difference into JAAA and USFR, which are the same liquidity with a coupon that follows the Fed up. What I did NOT do is re-establish a short. The BTC perp short is the only reason this book is -1.45% while it should have been grinding, and in this engine a perp short earns no funding at all - it was a directional bet wearing a carry costume, with BTC now at ~$79.7k, funding still positive at ~10% annualised and open interest up 6% in three days. A carry mandate is not a licence to be short a trending asset. This book is now pure long-carry, and its worst realistic week is a few tenths of a percent.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-16/opus5_carry.json

    Two things changed since the 2026-09-08 leg, and only two. First, the Fed call I am positioned for got confirmed rather than refuted: August CPI printed +0.4% m/m and 3.4% y/y with core 0.1pp above forecast on an Iran-war energy shock, and fed funds futures now put a 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00% at 84-91% for the 2026-09-16 meeting under Chair Warsh, with Goldman and JPMorgan having moved to the hike. That vindicates the floating-rate core, so I am adding to it rather than rotating away. Second, and this is the real reassessment: the compensation for sitting in mezzanine CLO paper has gone negative. High-yield OAS is 2.65%, essentially cycle tights, while the CCC-to-single-B differential has blown out past 600bp after widening ~200bp year to date, private credit funds are gating redemptions and marks are going from par to zero. That is a bifurcated market where the index level hides the loss tail, and BBB/BB CLO tranches are precisely the levered claim on that tail. CLOZ is the empirical proof: it has run a ~7.5% distribution yield and is still down 1.69% year to date, which means spread widening has already eaten more than the entire coupon. A carry manager's job is to harvest compensated spread, not to collect a coupon that the mark is quietly taking back, so CLOZ goes to zero weight. Third housekeeping point: USFR now distributes ~3.81% gross, ~3.66% net of its 15bp fee, and even after the hike resets it to roughly 3.75% net it still sits below the 4% APY this book earns on idle cash with no fee, no bid-ask and no mark-to-market noise. Cash strictly dominates that leg, so USFR goes to zero and cash rises to 16%. Net effect is that blended book yield only falls from about 6.0% to about 5.8% while I have removed the one position carrying genuine tail risk and the one position that was being paid less than cash. I deliberately kept the turnover surgical: JAAA, AMLP, FLOT and SPYI all stay, so only about a quarter of the book actually trades. This book has now run seven legs in nine weeks and is at -1.59% while earning positive carry the whole way, which tells me the churn has been the enemy, not the positioning. I am not rebuilding; I am cutting two legs and letting the rest compound.

  9. 2026-09-30REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-30/opus5_carry.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-30/opus5_carry.json

    Three things changed my mind since the 2026-09-16 leg. First, the hiking cycle is confirmed and extending: the Fed went to 3.75-4.00% on 09-16 in a 12-0 vote with 16 of 18 dots showing another hike, markets price ~65% for 10-28 and ~4.2% by December, with more into 2027. Against that, the engine pays a FIXED 4% APY on cash while SOFR-linked coupons reset upward at every hike. Cash is therefore a decaying asset in relative terms and floating-rate credit mechanically widens its advantage with each meeting. I cut cash 16%->10% and put the proceeds into AAA CLO. Second, FLOT no longer earns its place: it yields ~4.3% against a 4.0% risk-free engine cash rate, so I was accepting IG corporate credit and spread risk for roughly 30bps. That is the same logic this strategy already used to reject a Treasury floater, applied consistently - FLOT is sold in full and replaced by ICLO (Invesco AAA CLO Floating Rate Note ETF, 30-day SEC yield ~5.57%, 0.19% ER, $588mm AUM, $25.59 on 09-28), which pays ~125bps more for equal-or-better credit standing, since senior AAA CLO tranches sit above IG bank paper in the capital structure. Splitting the CLO core across Janus and Invesco also diversifies manager and deal-selection risk rather than concentrating it in one book. Third, I re-read why AMLP is down 3.29% while Brent trades ~$102: it is not trading as oil beta, it is trading as a yield instrument being repriced by rising short rates. At a 6.05% distribution it offers only ~50bps over a 5.57% AAA CLO floater while carrying full equity and commodity risk - poor compensation on carry grounds. So I size it as the hedge it is rather than as a carry engine: 20%->16%. I keep it, because the inflation the Fed is fighting IS energy, midstream posted record Q2 throughput, and it is the only leg that participates if oil keeps running. Net effect: blended carry rises from ~5.4% to ~5.8% annualized, the 66% floating block resets higher at every hike, and equity/commodity beta falls. Turnover is ~38% one-way at 2bps, roughly 2bps of NAV, which the added carry repays in under three weeks. I also widened the stops on the CLO legs from -5% to -8%. A AAA CLO fund's worst historical drawdown is ~2-3%, so a -5% stop is never hit by noise but could fire in exactly the liquidity air pocket where selling par-paying paper at the low is the worst possible action. This book's single lifetime standing-order fill was a stop that took it out of BTC-USD before a +30.68% rally; I will not repeat that error on instruments that redeem at par. -8% remains a genuine brake on a structured-credit catastrophe.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_dispersion.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, low-beta equity curve - roughly 7-9% annualised book volatility, drawdowns in the 4-6% range, and returns that will look dull against SPY in any strong beta rally and good against SPY in a flat or falling tape. The realistic base case is mid-single-digit annualised excess over cash if the current 1st-percentile correlation regime persists, and roughly flat if it does not. Management: re-run the idiosyncratic-volatility and pairwise-correlation screen every Friday and replace the bottom two or three names rather than holding a stale basket, since the out-of-sample evidence says the refreshed procedure works better than the fixed list; re-estimate the basket's beta weekly and resize the SPY/QQQ short to keep net beta inside +/-0.15, tolerating a small net short rather than a net long given that correlation is far more likely to rise than fall from 0.08. The trade I am watching for is a correlation spike: if the rolling 63-day average pairwise correlation moves back above 0.20, the dispersion premise is gone, the basket and the shorts converge, and I would cut gross exposure toward cash rather than try to ride it out. The dominant risk is a correlated selloff, in which every long falls together, the hedge only offsets its beta share, and the residual +0.10 net long plus the basket's higher-than-index volatility both work against me at once.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 +19.48%; 2025H2 +0.87%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -4.33%; 2025H2 -5.62%

    Engine runs: python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> on this exact book. A third window, 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30, returned +1.35% with a -5.17% max drawdown against SPY +6.31%. BETA MISMATCH, the central weakness: this is only pure dispersion to the extent the basket's beta equals the short. The equal-weight basket's beta to SPY is 1.02 on the 126-day lookback but 1.22 pooled over 2024-01 to 2026-07 (window range 1.02-1.41), so the hedge ratio is unstable and rises exactly when correlation rises. Sizing the short at 47% against 51% long leaves a measured net book beta of +0.107 (2024H1), +0.145 (2024H2), +0.117 (2025H1), +0.190 (2025H2) and -0.034 (2026H1), pooled +0.102, with book volatility 7.4% annualised and correlation to SPY +0.22 pooled. DECOMPOSITION of pre-cost gross return: 2026H1 +20.25% = -0.33% directional + 20.57% idiosyncratic; 2025H2 +1.50% = +2.76% directional - 1.26% idiosyncratic; 2025H1 +2.02% = +0.78% directional + 1.24% idiosyncratic. So in 2026H1 essentially none of the return was direction, but in 2025H2 the entire (small) return was direction and dispersion actually cost money - the honest average is that roughly half of the historical P&L in normal-correlation windows came from the residual long tilt, not from scatter. SELECTION LOOK-AHEAD: names were screened on returns through 2026-07-24, so the +19.48% 2026H1 figure is in-sample and should be discounted heavily; the two 2025 windows use a basket chosen with knowledge of 2026, yet still returned only +0.87% and +1.35%, which is the more sober estimate of what a stale basket does. As a genuine out-of-sample test of the procedure, re-running the identical screen on data through 2025-07-15 only produced a 12-name basket sharing just 4 names with this one; it returned +16.69% versus SPY +9.87% in 2025H2 and +4.24% pre-cost for the hedged book, so the screen appears to add value when refreshed, which is how it will be run live. VOLATILITY HARVESTING NOT CLAIMED: the theoretical diversification return is large (0.5 x (mean constituent variance 60.9%^2 - basket variance 22.7%^2) = 16.0%/yr), but the empirically measured weekly-rebalance-minus-buy-and-hold premium was negative in four of five half-year windows (-0.05%, -10.32%, +0.89%, -1.95%, -6.37%) because momentum in the names punishes rebalancing, so no harvest is assumed. Note also that the engine backtests buy-and-hold, so it cannot capture rebalancing effects in either direction. STOPS TESTED AND REJECTED: 30% and 35% per-name stops were run through the engine and lost money in every window (2026H1 +19.48% fell to +14.05%/+15.56%, 2025H2 +0.87% fell to -0.06%/+0.87%, 2025H1 +1.35% fell to -0.97%/-0.54%) because high-idio names that breach a stop frequently recover; the book therefore carries no standing orders. COSTS included by the engine: 3% APR borrow on the 47% short (1.41%/yr drag), 4% APY on 2% cash, 2bps per side entry on ~98% gross. Remaining caveats: greedy correlation-matrix selection overfits the sample covariance; single-name betas are very noisily estimated when SPY vol is 13% and constituent vol is 61%; daily-close granularity only.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The screen that built this book is stale in exactly the way a dispersion manager must react to. Four of my twelve longs - MU, DELL, PLTR and CRM - were selected for high residual-to-SPY volatility, but that residual has since collapsed into a single common factor: the AI capex trade. SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

    What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

    On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

    I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.
